Business.title: US borrowing costs hit 5% for first time since 2023 amid bond sell-off
Business.text:
US government borrowing costs have risen to 5% for the first time since 2023 as soaring oil prices fuelled by the war in the Middle East trigger an intensifying sell-off in the global bond market.

The yield – in effect the interest rate – on 10-year US Treasury bonds hit the psychologically important threshold on Monday, on a day of renewed selling pressure on Wall Street as the global oil price reached $108 a barrel.

With traders awaiting a crunch US Federal Reserve interest rate decision on Wednesday, the benchmark rate has steadily climbed from a low this year of 4% before the outbreak of the US-Israeli war on Iran in late February. The yield was last above 5% in October 2023.

It comes as the rising global oil price stokes inflation fears, with the latest move prompted by a series of drone attacks that have forced Saudi Arabia to close a vital east-west crude pipeline as the fallout from the war mounts.

Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, surged to more than $108.5 a barrel on Monday – a 3.7% increase on the day.

The spike came after Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi forces launched several attacks against Saudi Arabia and captured the strategic island of Perim in the Bab al-Mandab strait on Sunday, expanding their control of the waterway.

The rise was also fuelled by the Gulf states postponing a meeting with Tehran to discuss creating a temporary shipping lane through the strait of Hormuz, a vital channel through which a fifth of the world’s oil and gas supply normally passes.

Traders in the kingdom have warned it will run out of oil stocks for export if it does not reopen the east-west pipeline within days.

Gas prices also climbed higher on Monday, with the UK benchmark rising by 5% to 208.73p a therm – its highest level since December 2022.

It came despite Donald Trump on Monday announcing a deal between Ukraine and Russia not to hit each other’s energy targets, while insisting that he believed a politically sensitive rise in US diesel fuel prices was being driven by the conflict in Europe rather than the war in Iran.

With fears mounting as the Middle East war escalates, bond markets have come under intense selling pressure. The US 10-year Treasury yield is used in global financial markets as a benchmark for pricing other assets, meaning a jump in borrowing costs for Washington has consequences for countries, businesses and households worldwide.

Borrowing costs also rose across Europe on Monday, including a rise in 30-year UK government yields to the highest level since March 1998.

The moves come as traders await decisions on interest rates from the US Federal Reserve on Wednesday and the Bank of England on Thursday after the European Central Bank raised borrowing costs last week.

With investors anticipating an increase from the Fed and a hold decision from Threadneedle Street amid mounting inflationary pressures, analysts said global bond markets could face another week of renewed volatility.

Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “Markets are starting the week on a defensive footing, with the combination of another escalation in the Middle East and increasingly hawkish central-bank expectations weighing on risk appetite.”

With wholesale energy prices on the rise, the cost of petrol and diesel hit new Iran war highs on Monday, according to the RAC, with the average cost of petrol climbing to 169.68p and diesel hitting 191.68p.

The US-Israeli war with Iran has disrupted oil and gas supply across the Middle East this year, sending the oil price soaring from its prewar level of about $72 a barrel to peak at $126 in April.

Brent crude later fell back over the summer amid hopes of a lasting ceasefire, before starting to climb again after the memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran fell apart.

After a recent stepping-up of hostilities the benchmark again rose above the $100 a barrel threshold last week for the first time since July.

Chris Beauchamp, of the broker IG, said a “move back to the spring highs” looked increasingly likely. “Oil markets are being subjected to their worst fears all at once – attacks on energy infrastructure, the closure of Hormuz and a breakdown in attempts to restart negotiations,” he said.

“The risk of further disruption is also spreading beyond the Gulf, with the threat of renewed Houthi attacks on shipping adding another layer of uncertainty around key energy and trade routes.

“The major surprise is how calm markets remain in the face of all this, but if prices breach the March highs, things could get ugly very quickly.”

Business.title: OpenAI boss and Elon Musk back calls to put brakes on ‘reckless’ AI development
Business.text:
Sam Altman and Elon Musk have backed a call from the head of Anthropic, Dario Amodei, to “slow the pace” of AI development after he warned that an AI swarm could otherwise become capable of “taking over the entire internet” within a year.

In a rare show of unity, the rival technology leaders threw their weight behind the appeal from the founder and chief executive of the artificial intelligence company Anthropic, which came after a series of warnings from AI researchers last week. Amodei also called for safety coordination with China.

But the US president, Donald Trump, on a visit to his golf course in Ireland, played down the warnings and said “very negative forces” were “bringing up things that won’t happen”.

“We’re leading China in AI,” he said. “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly I want to ⁠keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins.

Amodei laid out his thoughts on “why the AI industry should slow down”, in an essay with a three-part plan for doing so, starting with giving independent monitors constant access to developers’ research processes. Amodei said “building [AI] too fast is reckless” and he feared that after hundreds of OpenAI agents hacked into the Hugging Face website this summer, a swarm with greater capabilities but similarly misaligned could cause hundreds of billions of dollars of damage by “taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet”. This was disputed by some AI experts as not particularly plausible and to be treated with scepticism.

Musk, the founder of Tesla and SpaceX, responded to Amodei’s slowdown plan with a series of posts on X: “Dario is right.”

He said: “I’ve been sounding the alarm on AI for a long time,” and referred to a 2014 post where he said: “We need to be super careful with AI. Potentially more dangerous than nukes.”

Amodei’s call comes as Anthropic prepares to float on the US stock market, in what is expected to be the biggest initial public offering of all time. It is expected to start marketing its planned $2tn-plus (£1.5tn) IPO soon.

Sam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI, responded to Amodei’s comments on Saturday. “I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier,” he said in a post on X. “Committing to having independent evaluators with employee-like access is a great idea, and we will do the same. We’ll have more to share soon.”

He also said OpenAI would not go public in 2026, citing safety concerns over artificial intelligence.

“I actually think that, given everything happening with safety, right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public, and we don’t feel pressure on that,” Altman told Fortune. Asked why he, Amodei, Musk, and the chief executives of Meta and Google did not sit down and “get on the same page” about a collective slowdown, he said: “I think that will happen.”

Demis Hassabis, a co-founder and chair of Google Deep Mind, also said: “The details need working through, but the direction is correct for meeting this critical moment.”

But some safety experts questioned whether Amodei’s plan went far enough. David Krueger, an AI professor, safety campaigner and former founding director of the UK government’s AI Security Institute, said: “We need an immediate, indefinite, international moratorium on frontier AI development.”

Amodei’s plan seeks a waiver from the US government to allow the frontier AI companies to coordinate without being punished for anti-competitive collusion. But David Sacks, a co-chair of Donald Trump’s council of advisers on science and technology, said: “Stop pretending you need anyone else’s permission … Stop pretending the motivation to slow down is purely altruistic. You face massive product-liability exposure if your products enable a truly damaging cyber-attack.”

Meanwhile, King Charles is preparing to meet leading figures from the most prominent AI companies on Thursday to ask them how the technology can be developed under the theme “AI for good”. One session is set to be called “prudence at the frontier”, which is expected to explore the possibility for clear red lines on the uses of AI to create bioweapons and launch cyber-attacks on critical systems.

Those expected to attend the event overseen by the Ditchley Foundation, which has drawn up a draft charter for AI leaders, include: senior executives at OpenAI and Anthropic; the Nvidia chief executive, Jensen Huang; Hassabis; Niccolo de Masi, the chair and chief executive of IonQ,; and Paolo Benanti, an adviser to the pope on issues of AI and technology ethics

The OpenAI researcher Aidan McLaughlin called Amodei’s essay “excellent” and said he agreed “with basically every word”.

Amodei said his company would “unilaterally” commit to the first of the steps, saying Anthropic would provide “third-party evaluators with permanent, employee-level access to our systems, so that they can verify adherence to our safety measures, report on incidents, and assess models’ alignment during training”.

Growing numbers of US lawmakers ​are calling for new rules to govern AI systems after cases of AI agents going rogue to hack external systems and AI ​safety researchers quitting their companies over concerns about the technology’s risks.

Politicians, both Democrats and Republicans, have responded with alarm and calls for more action. At the weekend the New York Times reported that Barack Obama on Thursday privately urged the Democrats to prioritise AI oversight in their agenda, telling party leaders on Thursday: “This is something that is moving very fast in private hands, and if we don’t get on top of it, I think can be dangerous.”

The former British prime minister Rishi Sunak, who advises Anthropic, wrote on Sunday: “We have had a wake-up call to take AI safety more seriously, to work out how to set limits on research. If governments don’t heed this, the risk of a serious accident will become unacceptably high.”

On Wednesday, a former Anthropic employee had warned that AI could precipitate human extinction by 2030. The researcher, Jacob Coxon, said in a series of posts that he had quit his job because Anthropic and his previous employer, OpenAI, were ignoring or mishandling their response to the threat AI posed.

Asked to comment on his former employee’s view, Amodei said: “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him … I think there’s some chance that things go wrong but it’s not all that high.”

“I am not a doomer about this,” he told CNN. “I think this technology can be built safely.”

Business.title: Tensions simmer on US-Canada border for two towns relying on each other
Business.text:
Like many Canadians, Tom Reid isn’t crossing the US-Canada border as often these days. But he needed a haircut.

The woman who cuts his hair lives in International Falls, Minnesota – her “sister is married to my wife’s cousin”, he explained – and so Reid, whose duty free shop in Fort Frances, Ontario, has to travel to her.

That’s how it goes for the residents of the two towns, divided by the Rainy River and an international border. They’re longtime friends and, in many cases, family. People cross the border frequently to shop, dine, go bowling, take their kids to sports and visit each other.

But Trump’s trade war against the US’s northern neighbor, and his derogatory comments about their country, has Canadians – known for their politeness – angry. Furious, actually. They’re shopping less at US businesses, and, in an unusual show of patriotism, encouraging consumers to “buy Canadian instead”.

Reid is buying Canadian more and more, he said at the register in his shop, with the Canadian flag on the wall behind him. “I don’t have that much choice, eh?” he said.

American business owners have seen declines in Canadian sales, while grappling with the uncertainty and costs associated with tariffs on their products. With tourist season winding down, and the leaves starting to change into yellows and oranges, the two towns are quieter.

Canada’s retaliatory tariffs went into force this week, though no one who lived in the towns had seen that directly reflected in prices yet. It was the latest heated battle between the two countries in the last nearly two years.

The mayors of the two towns call each other friends, and signed a joint declaration in 2025 affirming that friendship after Trump retook the White House. The flags of Minnesota, Ontario, both towns, and both countries fly outside the town offices in Fort Frances. But there’s only so much – and really, nothing – that a local official can do to blunt the economic effects of slipshod tariffs put in place by one man, more than a thousand miles away in Washington.

Hoping for the best

Most Canadians recognize this, according to Andrew Hallikas, the mayor of Fort Frances. They like Americans, and Fort Frances residents can relate to Minnesotans a lot: they share similar interests, in the outdoors and in community, he said. But they’re “irate” at Trump – for bullying their country, for going against an ally – and for suggesting Canada should become the 51st US state.

“You cannot imagine how angry that makes us,” Hallikas said. “Please quote me on this. I cannot make this clear enough: we will never become the 51st state. We consider ourselves to probably be the best country in the world in which to live, and we’re quite content to remain that way, thank you very much.”

For two towns that rely on each other, the tension of the trade war simmers underneath the surface. They all want it to end. They don’t know how, or when, it will.

As the Guardian interviewed the mayor of International Falls at a coffee shop on the town’s main drag, a Fort Frances resident interjected angrily to tell the mayor that Canadians are “so pissed off” at Trump for how he’s attacked their country and that International Falls needed Canadians to survive. Their town was suffering, and their businesses losing longtime customers from Canada, because of it, he said.

“I’m originally from the Falls, but I’m an American living in Canada,” the man said. “I’m scared to put that American flag on my shirt, what he’s done.”

Residents, and the leaders of the towns, are worried about how they will rebuild the relationship between their two countries if this continues for much longer. Businesses will find other suppliers. Shoppers will replace their favorites with homegrown options. The sense of nationalism hardens.

“We just hope for the best at this point,” said the International Falls mayor, Drake Dill.

Grant Hauschild, a Democratic Minnesota state senator who represents 65% of the state’s border with Canada, said he’s heard from businesses that have lost up to 30% of their revenue from Canadians. With people already struggling with inflation and high costs, he said a hit like that goes from “a concern to devastation”.

“My hope is, of course, that the relationship goes back to normal once we pass these chaotic times,” Hauschild said. “I think that’s what really scares me most … Even if people want to go back to the way things were, they might have unfortunately kind of moved on – and moved beyond – the relationship.”

Two towns, one community

To cross the Rainy River into either side, people use a toll bridge, with the cost for an average car now $10. They present documents to customs agents on whichever side they’re entering, and answer questions about their purpose in town. People who cross regularly recognize the agents and ask after their families.

The main parts of each respective town sit on either side of the crossing, with both towns initially growing around paper mills. Fort Frances’ mill has since closed; International Falls’ is still running. Fort Frances is larger than International Falls, and because Canada is more sparse, Fort Frances serves as a regional hub. Its hospital will soon be getting an MRI machine – a huge boon for its aging population.

The shops on either side carry gifts from both countries, catering to tourists who fly in to fish, mostly for walleye, and largely on the Canadian side. In a Fort Frances store, kids books called “Little Minnesota” and “Little Canada” sat right beside each other on a shelf. In International Falls, shelves of souvenir cups carried designs for International Falls and Canada.

While Canadian flags line the shop windows and fly throughout downtown Fort Frances, Hallikas said this is not a reflection of increased patriotism, but just a border town welcoming visitors to their country. The two towns are “neighbors by geography, but we are friends by choice”, he said.

“The bridge is over 100 years old, and we’ve been going back and forth it for over 100 years,” Hallikas said. “Before that, there was a ferry. But our friendship is still going to exist when Trump is long gone.”

Dill, the International Falls mayor, owned a business and lived in Canada for 11 years. Many of his friends are Canadian. This fall, he will go up to an island in Canada to meet up with friends.

“There’s no politics in that. There’s no thought of exchange rate, or trade war, or tariffs. It’s just – we’re friends,” he said. “But then you come home and you talk and you watch the news. … I would be really disappointed if it gets to a point where we can’t work through it, and there’s a fundamental change that will hurt International Falls significantly.”

Residents on both sides have favorite products they grab whenever they cross. For Heather Johnson, executive director of the Fort Frances chamber of commerce, it’s Top the Tater, an iconic Minnesota chive and onion dip. She also checks prices on cheeses, and peruses the wider variety of pastas for sale in US stores. Johnson bowls weekly in a league in International Falls, made up of both Americans and Canadians.

Leanne Guba, a Canadian who owns Hometown Hobby and Crafts in International Falls, crosses back into her home country once or twice a month, usually walking across the bridge, to buy ketchup chips, chocolate bars and Dad’s brand oatmeal chocolate chip cookies.

American liquor is no longer on the shelves at government-run Ontario liquor stores, by order of Premier Doug Ford. The push to buy Canadian is “pretty well elbows-up”, Johnson said. “I’m drinking Canadian red wine now.”

‘Mr T took care of that’

Reid, the duty-free shop owner, said the tourist season was about average for him, with no noticeable decline in sales. He has seen some change in his customers.

A couple of years ago, they’d come in with the signature red Maga (Make America Great Again) hats. Last year, not as many. This year, he didn’t see any red hats, and customers would tell him they didn’t vote for Trump. They’ll ask about the missing American bourbon from his shelves, and he’ll tell them, “Mr T took care of that”.

He used to cross the border to go to a show, or the grocery store, or Menard’s, a hardware store, but not anymore. His daughter and her husband used to cross weekly for a date night and shopping, but no longer. People over here are “really upset” with Trump, he said. It has renewed his sense of Canadian pride, but “I’ve always had good pride”.

Johnson, whose kids are now grown, said: “I’m glad that my kids grew up knowing both countries, and they know that there really isn’t a difference in people.”

Across the border in International Falls, craft store owner Guba said she was seeing fewer Canadians, for several reasons. They’re dealing with rising costs, too, and the exchange rate is unfavorable. Some of it is politics, she said. Canadian regulars are coming less frequently.

“They’re definitely being a little more picky about when they come over or being more careful about what they buy,” she said.

The decline, while dealing with unpredictable tariffs on goods she brings in from overseas, has had an impact on her business. She’s adapted by seeking out new suppliers, bringing in new merchandise lines, and trying to reduce costs. She has a few companies she orders from in Canada – including a toy brand and a puzzle company – and expects the new tariffs will likely increase costs on those products.

People are upset about the political dynamics, but they don’t tend to vent their political frustrations openly, she said. There may be the odd joke here and there, but not usually full-blown political debate. “We tend to try to stay friendly,” she said.

The latest tourist season was “decent”, she said. “Overall, we’re still surviving … You can’t really control it.”

‘We remain neutral’

It’s tough to gauge the full impact of declining Canadian spending in the border town, though anecdotally, people are noticing it. The International Falls chamber of commerce would not comment on the impact of the tariffs on the town, or the deteriorating relationship between the two countries.

“We remain neutral on political matters so that we can best serve our diverse membership, which includes individuals and organizations with a wide range of views. Because of that, the Chamber does not have an official comment on the political issues surrounding the US-Canada relationship,” the chamber said in an email.

Isaac Johnson, who owns the Coffee Landing café in International Falls and lives above it with his wife, said he still sees a lot of Canadians who come over to grab espresso and breakfast. He loves his Canadian customers, including the couple he watched meet up at the coffee shop from across the border. They later married.

The locals are caught in the middle of political games, said Johnson, who tries to just focus on himself, his family, and his faith. But people do get emotional about it at times, and “if you definitely bring up politics, for sure,” he said – just as the man who confronted Dill, the mayor, did.

The man, who didn’t share his name or want to have a longer conversation with a reporter, said he’s noticed far fewer Canadians around town, nothing like it used to be. He described Canadians as “very pissed off” and said snowbirds were selling their houses in the US. International Falls voters went for Trump in 2024.

These broader issues, like the trade war, “pit us against each other”, Johnson said, noting that the man got mad at the mayor “over a guy that’s making billions off us all”.

“I love the Canadians, I love Americans, and I love them coming over here and enjoying what we have here, and we can go and enjoy what they have,” Johnson said.

Dill, the town’s mayor, said Canadians are “definitely” not coming to International Falls as much as they were, though he thinks it has more to do with the exchange rate. Still, he said later, “we need all the Canadian commerce we can get, and I would like to think they feel the same way”.

Local officials are in a tough position. They have no control over the tariffs, though with their communities at the center of the impact, they are expected to answer questions and concerns over levies. They have no direct line to the Trump administration, if that would even make a difference. And their communities are suffering.

Hope springs eternal

Hauschild, the Minnesota state senator, said he meets regularly with the Canadian consulate in St Paul, and reiterates his belief in a strong relationship with Canada. But as a state lawmaker, he has little to no control over any of it, beyond using his bully pulpit.

Hallikas, the Fort Frances mayor, said most Canadians have “no rancor for individual Americans” and treat them kindly when they visit, largely avoiding talking about Trump or American politics. Americans will have to work to undo the damage Trump has done to the relationship between the two countries, and that will take time, even after the trade war simmers down or ends, he said.

“But we’ll still be friends with the folks in Minnesota and International Falls,” Hallikas said.

Dill said he doesn’t often run into the frustrations directed at him by the man in the coffee shop, though it happens. He doesn’t have any way he can directly fix the issue.

“The US elected our current president and he has his own agenda and I don’t see that I can stop it,” he said. “I don’t want it to affect us locally. We’ll see. Hope springs eternal. I mean, I thought that everything was going along fine, but apparently it wasn’t.”

The uncertainty of it all is “frustrating”, and he’s most curious about where it all lands, when a truce could be signed so that businesses can have a sense of comfort in planning for their futures. The two countries are engaged in a heated dispute – or a “donnybrook,” as they would say in Canada, noted Dill.

He likened the current situation to two longtime best friends, who hunted and fished and vacationed together for years – until one of them said, you’ve been taking advantage of me for years.

“That’s like driving a nail in a fence,” he said, “and then you pull it out, and even if the fence still stands, there’s a hole where the nail was.”

Business.title: US consumers faced more high prices in August as Iran war raised energy costs
Business.text:
US consumer prices remained stubbornly high in August as the end of the ceasefire between the US and Iran pushed energy prices up, according to data from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics released on Friday.

The annualized inflation rate was 3.4%, the same as it was in July. The most recent peak was seen in May, when the inflation rate hit a three-year high at 4.2%. Core inflation, which strips out volatile energy and food prices, increased 0.3% from the month before and 2.4% annually.

Gasoline increased 27.4% compared with the year before, accounting for more than one-third of the overall monthly increase in prices. Fuel , which is used to power and heat homes, increased annually at a staggering 52%.

Prices of common grocery store essentials, such as meat, poultry, eggs and dairy, increased slightly, from 0.1% to 0.3%. Lettuce prices continued to fall, probably continued fallout from the cyclosporiasis outbreak.

Despite dipping from its most recent peak, inflation remained above levels that were seen before the war in Iran, largely because of higher energy prices. On Friday, the cost of diesel, used for trucks, buses and trains, rose past $6 a gallon for the first time ever. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, also surpassed $108 on Friday, its highest level since May. Meanwhile, gas prices at the pump sat at an average of $4.29 a gallon, $1.10 higher than the average a year ago, according to AAA.

It’s a worrying sign for Republicans, who are on the ballot at a time when consumer sentiment has hit record lows and Americans say they are struggling to afford gas and groceries. Concerns over inflation have also bled into the US bond market, where the yields on some US treasurys have reached their highest points since the 2008 recession. Yet it’s unclear when relief will come.

The White House is aware of what this could mean for the upcoming elections. On Wednesday night, Trump said Americans would get a $5,000 “dividend” if Republicans win a majority in the midterms, which critics said was akin to bribery.

One of the most direct ways the federal government can affect prices comes from the power of the US Federal Reserve, which sets the interest rates that have an effect on the price of loans, including mortgages, car payments and student debt.

With prices remaining stubbornly high and core inflation rising, Friday’s report bolsters the likelihood that the Fed will vote to increase rates at its board meeting next week.. Either move could have heavy implications for the US economy.

In a social media post last week, Trump said the central bank “must get smart” and lower rates. “A STRONG COUNTRY MEANS A LOWER INTEREST RATE,” he declared.

But pressure to increase rates has been growing. At the Fed’s last board meeting in July, it voted 9-3 to maintain rates – the first time in a decade that three board members shared dissent over a policy decision.

Historically, raising interest rates helps to lower inflation – making investments more expensive slows the economy. Inflation reached 9.1%, a 40-year high, in 2022. After the Fed spent the next few years increasing interest rates, up to a range of 5.25%-5.5%, inflation went down to 2.3% in April 2025.

Interest rates now sit at a range of 3.5%-3.75%, two percentage points lower than where they were two years ago. With inflation back up, some Fed economists have said it might be time for higher interest rates.

Last week, the Fed governor Christopher Waller said there was “considerable uncertainty about how military conflicts, trade policy, and artificial intelligence will affect prices and economic activity” and it might be appropriate to raise rates if inflation showed no signs of easing.

“If there is continued progress toward our 2% goal, then I am willing to support holding the policy rate at its current level,” he said at a Reuters event. “But if inflation comes in hot, I would consider a rate hike.”

The Fed’s new chair, Kevin Warsh, has made it clear the central bank will combat inflation during his tenure and achieve price stability. During a closely watched speech in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, last month, Warsh said that underlying inflation trends had not “meaningfully improved” over the summer.

“We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed. Otherwise, we have work to do,” Warsh said.

Business.title: Iran’s Houthi allies capture strategic island on vital oil shipping route
Business.text:
Yemen’s rampant Houthi forces have captured the strategic island of Perim in the Bab al-Mandab strait, expanding their control of the narrow waterway, one of the ​world’s vital shipping routes.

The Iran-aligned Houthis took control of the volcanic island after forces allied to the UN-backed, Aden-based government left in the latest of a dramatic series of reverses along Yemen’s west coast in recent days, including the loss of the port city of Mocha on Thursday.

Saudi Arabia, which supports and bankrolls the official Yemen government, mounted air raids on Houthi positions in Mocha on Friday.

The Bab al-Mandab strait links Asia to Europe via the Red Sea and Suez canal. Perim island, also known as Mayun, divides the waterway in two, close to its narrowest point. The United Arab Emirates, a former Saudi ally in the anti-Houthi coalition, had been building an airbase on the island before ending its active involvement in the conflict in January.

Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab to export its crude since Iran has been targeting vessels in the strait of Hormuz. About 12% of the world’s goods are typically shipped through the strait.

Saudi Arabia has now said it has shut down a crucial pipeline a day after it was attacked by drones, and Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels captured Perim.

It said it had shut its East-West pipeline as “a precautionary measure”, blaming the attack on several drones that came from Iraq. In a statement carried by the state-run Saudi Press Agency, the kingdom said it would not respond to the attack to give the Iraqi government “an opportunity to take the necessary measures”.

The pipeline, also known as the Petroline, runs for 1,201km (746 miles) from the Abqaiq oilfield in the kingdom’s east near Bahrain and Qatar, to the port city Yanbu at the Red Sea.

Built in the 1980s, it has played an important role in Saudi Arabia’s ability to export oil after the disruption of the strait of Hormuz during the Iran war.

Full Houthi control of shipping in the Bab al-Mandab strait, alongside Iranian control of the strait of Hormuz, would strengthen the chokeholds of anti-western forces over global energy shipments. Oil prices have risen to more than $100 a barrel as the fighting in Yemen has escalated.

Iran hailed the Houthi advances in an official statement on Friday, its first extended comment on the renewed fighting inside Yemen. Iran and the Houthis have been allied since the Houthis rose to power inside Yemen in 2014.

In a statement the Houthis hailed the expulsion of “Saudi enemy” troops from six districts in the Taiz and Hodeidah regions, the capture of 4,500 sq miles, the targeting of “seven military divisions of the Saudi enemy’s forces” and the “killing, capture, and wounding” of hundreds of soldiers. It also claimed to have released hundreds of prisoners “held by the Saudi enemy’s mercenaries for years”.

British diplomatic sources said they did not at present expect Donald Trump to sanction any US bombing of Houthi positions in Yemen, despite requests to do so from Saudi Arabia. The pace of the Houthi advance, and political divisions in the Yemen governorates not controlled by the Houthis, have left western capitals fearful that even the Yemen government capital, Aden, could fall to the Houthis. The UK effectively treated Yemen as a British protectorate until 1967.

The Houthi offensive has cost more than 500 lives and displaced about 46,000 people, the UN migration agency said on Friday.

The Houthi progress down the Red Sea coast from the port of Hodeidah also strengthens Iran’s hand in trying to reach an agreement with other Gulf states on future control of the strait of Hormuz, the central dispute between the US and Iran. Iran has reached an agreement on temporary approved routes with Oman, the country sharing the southern coast of the Hormuz strait. The proposed deal is supposed to be discussed at a meeting of Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) foreign ministers in the Omani coastal city of Salalah on Monday.

The deal, including a temporary approved route for shipping largely under Iranian control, would – if agreed by the GCC – put pressure on the US to lift its highly effective blockade of Iranian oil ports, which is severely damaging the Iranian economy.

The US struck a surprise ceasefire deal with the Houthis in May 2025 after the cost of a bombing campaign escalated, and Houthis gave private assurances that they would not attack US shipping in the Red Sea. The Houthi leadership this week continued to give similar assurances to all shipping except Saudi Arabian oil tankers.

On 14 August Saudi Arabia assembled a 14-country international maritime naval coalition to protect freedom of navigation in the Bab al-Mandab strait and the Gulf of Aden. The coalition, including Bahrain, Pakistan, Somalia, Djibouti, Turkey and Egypt, has so far been invisible, though Riyadh would argue that such a coalition of the willing takes time to assemble.

Recriminations are under way over the fall of Mocha, with the role of Maj Gen Tareq Saleh, the leader of the National Resistance Forces that retreated from the city, under scrutiny. He said the retreat was necessary to regroup his forces.

On her Facebook page, the Yemeni 2011 Nobel peace prize winner, Tawakkol Karman, called on Yemen’s president, Rashad al-Alimi, to dismiss Saleh and to refer him for investigation and trial on charges of conspiracy and high treason.

Amr al-Bidh, the foreign affairs representative of the separatist political organisation the Southern Transitional Council (STC), said he had warned western diplomats repeatedly of the need for a comprehensive national regional and international strategy to defeat the Houthis, adding occasional airstrikes were not enough.

He accused the Saudis of strategic incompetence and of alienating the southern forces most needed to combat the Houthis.

“The position is now very serious,” he said. “The Houthis’ presence in the strait means they will be able to control the waterways without needing to use sophisticated weapons that as a result they can now use elsewhere. The advance is also likely to give them a new income through control of ports along the west coast of the Red Sea.” The Houthis are already offering concessionary rates to draw traffic from ports controlled by the Yemeni government in the Gulf of Aden.

The STC was the dominant political and military force in southern Yemen until this January, when Saudi Arabia bombed its troops, closed its political organisation down and detained as many as 20 of its leaders in Riyadh.

A Saudi promise of a dialogue about the southern question made in January has never been kept, al-Bidh said, adding that Human Rights Watch warned in a March report that some pro-STC protests in Aden were being repressed with undue violence.

“The betrayal of promises had left the southern population unwilling to leave their home territories to fight the Houthis in the north,” he said. “The Saudis for 10 years have been dependent on the people of the south to deter the Houthis, and the STC with as many as 80,000 troops at its disposal, has been the backbone of that force.”

Saudi Arabia is facing a familiar dilemma: whether to reach a negotiated settlement with the Houthis on the future of Yemen or to try to push the highly stretched Houthi forces back.

Although the Houthis operate independently of Tehran’s instructions, it is hugely to Iran’s advantage for them to be fighting Saudi Arabia, as the Saudis are more likely in turn to put pressure on Washington to relent over Iran.

Sports.title: Sydney Sweeney: Athletes including Amy Hunt respond to controversial advert
Sports.text:
Female athletes have spoken out against a controversial sports gambling advert starring actress Sydney Sweeney.

The advert has gone viral online and features American Sweeney naked but covering parts of her body with various pieces of sporting equipment.

It has sparked a strong reaction, with many female athletes criticising its sexualisation of women in sport, and how they are being defined by their appearance rather than their achievements as sportswomen.

Amy Hunt, who became a four-time European champion earlier this summer, referenced the advert after she ran a season's best 22.10 seconds to finish fourth in the 200m final at the Ultimate Championship in Budapest on Sunday.

"Sydney Sweeney, this is what women in sport look like," Hunt said in her post-race interview with BBC Sport.

Referring to Melissa Jefferson-Wooden's winning time of 21.47 seconds, the fourth fastest ever over the distance, she added: "21.4. Muscles. Hard work, blood, sweat, tears. This is a beautiful evening."

American actress Sweeney, 29, starred in the television series Euphoria and her films include Anyone But You and The Housemaid.

The backlash has included many other athletes from a range of sports posting videos of themselves competing or training, and describing the frustrations and struggles they have faced throughout their careers.

The trend was started by American gymnast Gracie Kramer, who posted a montage of herself training with the caption, "I don't know what Sydney Sweeney was doing, but this is what women in sport look like."

Kramer told BBC World Service's Newshour show she "did not expect" the reaction to her post and "just wanted to uplift women and remind them that you may see these types of ads but remember that this is not the only thing that matters".

She said it was "so cool" to see "all the incredible athletes hopping on this trend, uplifting themselves, uplifting each other", adding she was used to getting "very demeaning and objectifying" messages from men because of competing in a leotard as a gymnast.

Kramer added: "Unfortunately being objectified pretty much my entire career, it made me feel strong enough to post about this and to stand up for the women that don't want to be objectified and don't want to be looped into this unfortunate narrative that's been pushed for a long time."

Australia's four-time Olympic swimming champion Ariarne Titmus said: "Not only is it a kick in the face to every woman who has dedicated her life to perfecting her craft, but every woman who enjoys sports for what it really is.

"How do we live in a world where monetising a woman's body and sexualising women's sport is still a thing?"

British cyclist and Olympic champion Sophie Capewell MBE, rugby players Lisa Neumann and Ellie Boatman and Australian water polo Olympian Tilly Kearns also shared their stories.

"I think it's quite powerful, the amount of women who've come out and said something," Capewell told BBC Sport after her post gained attention.

"It's giving a very specific picture of women around sport and I think that's the challenging thing. Why is that the face of the campaign that is associated with sport?

"And that's the way you want to portray a woman, instead of it having, I don't know, an athlete or anything else that's more sport-centric?

"It's not necessarily that people are upset with someone having autonomy, it's the fact that that seems to be the only narrative that is directed around women in sports, or that's what gets more popularity."

England women's rugby player Alex Matthews said adverts like Sweeney's should not make young women believe there is a "one size fits all" body.

"You don't get that idolised perfect body," she told BBC Sport. "Especially in rugby - you wouldn't have a team.

"Every body type has a strength."

Matthews, who represented Great Britain in rugby sevens at Tokyo 2020, said one of "most inspiring" things about being in the Olympic village was seeing "the older generations, the younger generations, the taller people, the you know slightly bigger people, but they were all the best at what they did".

Sports.title: Manchester derby VAR officials not given Premier League game at weekend
Sports.text:
The video assistant referee for the Manchester derby, Matt Donohue, and his assistant VAR, Blake Antrobus, have not been appointed for this weekend's Premier League games.

The decision was made by the Premier League refereeing body Pro Ref's chief refereeing officer Howard Webb and the management team.

It follows Pro Ref admitting to an "error of judgement" in awarding Erling Haaland's winning goal for Manchester City at Manchester United on Sunday.

The striker scored in the 60th minute at Old Trafford when he turned in a shot at the back post from Josko Gvardiol's cross.

His effort was initially disallowed on the field for offside but, following VAR intervention, the goal was awarded as the Norwegian was ruled to have been played onside by Patrick Dorgu's boot.

However, there was debate as to whether the goal should have been disallowed for City midfielder Enzo Fernandez, who was in an offside position, interfering with play as he dived attempting to head the ball in a central position before Haaland's finish.

"It was established that Enzo Fernandez did not play the ball and therefore that makes any offside offence subjective," said Pro Ref in a statement.

"However, on this occasion, the VAR did not recognise the likely impact of his position and should have recommended an on-field review."

City, who had Phil Foden sent off after 23 minutes, maintained their 100% league record from four games with the victory.

Sports.title: Josh Kerr: Ultimate Championship 1500m winner ramps up debate over country vs brands kit
Sports.text:
After Josh Kerr became Great Britain's first ever Ultimate Champion with a dominant victory in the 1500m in Budapest on Sunday evening, he celebrated in customary fashion - Union Jack draped around him, beaming smile, arms raised before the cheering crowd.

But he also did something less traditional, ramping up a battle over funding at the top of athletics in the process.

The 28-year-old made a clear point of obscuring the Nike sponsor's logo on his Great Britain kit by tying his Brooks-branded running spikes over his shoulder, meaning that the video footage and photographs of his trophy lift highlighted his own personal sponsor rather than his nation's.

After praising the inaugural running of the Ultimate Championship, a new biennial event run by World Athletics with a focus on big names, Kerr explained the meaning behind the move in his interview with BBC Sport.

"There is one last thing that I think we can get right, which is allowing the athletes to represent their own brands versus their country," Kerr said.

"I love my country and competing for them, but we don't make any money from that sadly. We don't have the pay cheques that other sports do yet. So that would be an opportunity to grow."

BBC Sport has contacted World Athletics for comment.

Edinburgh native Kerr has won medals representing Great Britain at both the Olympics - picking up bronze in 2020 and silver in 2024 - and World Championships, having taken gold in 2023.

At those events, Kerr is directly representing his country - there are national medal tables in which the triumphs achieved by compatriots are tallied up together.

But at the Ultimate Championship a much smaller field of athletes are competing for individual titles in their respective events. There is no country medal table, and the new event is billed as a season finale for individual athletes after the conclusion of the Diamond League campaign.

In the Diamond League, athletes are free to show off their own sponsors who provide them with funding by wearing their own kits.

Kerr, and the other athletes who were crowned Ultimate Champions during the three-day competition in Hungary, earned $150,000 (£111,111) for winning.

But his pointed comments made plain the position athletes find themselves in.

Whereas players in sports like football earn a salary based on a contract with the team that employs them, and athletes in individual sports like tennis and golf can earn a great deal from prize money at major tournaments, athletics competitors rely much more heavily on personal sponsorships and endorsements.

That is because they are paid no direct annual salary, and the only standardised prize money on offer is $50,000 (£37,000) for winning gold in one of the 48 track and field events at the Olympics.

That prize money was only introduced at the 2024 Games in Paris, and is paltry compared to the potential millions in winnings on offer in other major sports.

Some nations - including the USA - also choose to pay athletes who win medals from their own resources, but Britain does not.

Instead, athletes are awarded funding and grants by UK Sport, with the majority of the money coming from the National Lottery.

UK Sport ranks athletes by how likely they are to win medals at major events, and gives more funding to those whose chances it believes are better.

Athletes typically use that funding to pay for training camps, equipment, travel and, in some cases, personal support staff like physiotherapists, nutritionists and chefs.

So why would athletes be instructed to wear national team kit at the Ultimates?

The Ultimate Championship is billed as three fast-paced evenings with a record $10m (£7.4m) prize pot on offer for the biggest stars in athletics.

The condensed schedule and focus on star names is designed to appeal to viewers on television and social media - the latter likely playing a role in the focus on short, sharp bursts of action which can capture attention online.

Most viewers of athletics are used to watching athletes compete while wearing national kit at the Olympics and World Championships. Put simply, the use of a national kit makes it easier for the casual viewer to quickly spot who they should be rooting for and feel invested in the action.

But Kerr's comments have highlighted the fact that something which may well improve the viewing experience can be felt as a direct financial negative by the athletes themselves.

With the next edition of the Ultimate Championship set to take place in September 2028, shortly after the Olympics in Los Angeles, the battle between brands and country could continue to heat up.

Sports.title: Spanish Grand Prix: Madrid F1 circuit set for changes after criticism
Sports.text:
Organisers of the Spanish Grand Prix are poised to make changes to the new Madrid circuit after criticism of its inaugural race at the weekend.

Drivers pointed out the lack of overtaking opportunities on the new Madring, with Williams' Alex Albon claiming the race was "pretty boring" and Audi's Gabriel Bortoleto saying he "almost fell asleep".

Drivers praised the track's challenge over a single lap, but world champion Lando Norris said one section was "useless" and it was "not a great racetrack".

But team bosses praised the new facility at the Ifema exhibition centre near Madrid's international airport.

And the organisers have told commercial rights holder F1 and governing body the FIA that they are prepared to make changes to the venue for next year.

Ferrari team principal Frederic Vasseur said: "First, I have to say that we can discuss about overtaking, but overall, for me, the event was mega.

"The infrastructure, we were mega welcome in the city. We have also to be fair with them and to congratulate Madrid for the job done on this side.

"They are keen to do modifications in the future. They have probably more latitude in Madrid than in Monaco to change something. Let's work together to see if we can do something. But overall, I think we have to be fair with them. It was a good effort."

And Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff said: "For a first [race], it's probably one of the best, or maybe the best, that I've seen so far. It's a temporary circuit. They've built something that is challenging for the drivers. A mini Macau or a mini Monaco. The location is good.

"We're thinking about how much more can we do next year in terms of the events here or presentations because we have the space and that's very rare. So I would say congratulations for a first.

"And then it's the tricky bit. Doing a track that is spectacular also for the drivers. And then building it in a way that there is lots of overtaking.

"I had a discussion yesterday with the CEO of the circuit and they are totally open-minded about next year and say we've had the discussions with the FIA - 'what is it we should do? How is it that we should lay the track out when it comes to overtaking also?'

"There is a constant discussion and I think that they are on it and understand that we can tweak it a little bit here or there."

Race winner Kimi Antonelli said: "It definitely doesn't create overtaking opportunities and it doesn't push you to try and make a move because 80% of the time you might have a contact.

"There are some corners that need to be changed to create more overtaking opportunities because right now, yes, it's nice over one lap, but for sure in the race you're just stuck behind."

And world champion Norris, who was denied victory for McLaren by the unfortunate timing of a virtual safety car, said: "There are some obvious changes they should make. They should get rid of [Turns] 18, 19 - useless. Just have more of a straight into a hairpin.

"I don't know how someone looks at this design and goes, 'mint'.

"There's a lot of opportunity. They can make it into a track that's good for racing, and I'm excited to come back here next year if they can make these changes because I think it's a track that is good fun to drive and it can be a great racetrack."

On social media, F1 fans also criticised access and the facilities, including having to sit on earth trackside, poor visibility, broken facilities and a general lack of readiness.

It is well known that organisers were up against it in terms of the timeframe to get the track ready for its first event.

The circuit is made up of a combination of roads already in place at Ifema and specific parts of permanent circuit, including the trademark banked corner at Turn 12 known as La Monumental.

Madring managing director Luis Garcia Abad, the former manager of two-time F1 world champion Fernando Alonso, did not respond to requests for comment from BBC Sport on Monday.

But after the race he told Autosport: "The FIA defined clearly which is the way to improve the track layout, and we will be open because we will have to reinstall the track for the next year.

"I really believe that the drivers enjoyed qualifying a lot. But for sure we will try to make an improvement for next year.

"We have the space, we have a venue, we have the facilities, we have the capacity to do it. I'm sure that FOM [Formula One Management], FIA and ourselves, we will try. If we can improve something, we will do it."

Sports.title: Premier League title race: Are Arsenal and Man City the only contenders?
Sports.text:
Four games is far too soon to be talking about who is in or out of the title race... isn't it?

And yet Arsenal and Manchester City, who have been the top two in three of the past four seasons, look a level above everyone else so far.

Is it already a two-horse race?

With new (or newish) managers, Manchester United, Chelsea, Liverpool and Tottenham were all looking for better things this season.

But so far their starts range from shaky to shambolic.

Arsenal and Manchester City are the only two teams with 12 points from four games.

They are already four points above third-placed Hull City - who despite their brilliant early form may not consider themselves in any kind of title equation - and five above the rest.

Arsenal are the defending champions and pre-season title favourites.

Under manager Mikel Arteta they ended a 22-year title drought last season with what was often perceived to be an attritional style of play.

They started this season with a hugely impressive 3-0 victory over Manchester City in the Community Shield.

And they have carried on with victories over Coventry, Aston Villa, Chelsea and Sunderland - plus Napoli in the Champions League.

Including last season, they are now on a nine-game winning run in the league - and last lost in any competition in 90 minutes to City on 19 April.

Unlike Arsenal, City do not have the continuity this season with boss Pep Guardiola leaving after six titles, including a Treble, in 10 years.

Enzo Maresca, once his assistant, has taken over and led them to four wins from four in the league after that loss in Cardiff to the Gunners.

They have beaten Bournemouth, Crystal Palace, Coventry - plus Porto in the Champions League - before their controversial 1-0 success at Manchester United on Sunday.

Erling Haaland scored the only goal, with the Premier League's refereeing body later admitting a mistake as it should have been ruled out for offside.

Despite their 100% starts, the underlying numbers behind Arsenal and City's starts do not imply total dominance.

Brighton (13) and Chelsea (10) have scored more goals than the eight that the top two have both netted.

For shots, Arsenal and City rank 10th and 11th and touches in the opposition box they are sixth and fifth respectively.

Arsenal have only conceded once and City have let in two goals - two of the best records in the league.

The next three favourites to win the title with most bookmakers - in order - were Chelsea, Liverpool and Manchester United - with Tottenham some way back.

Chelsea and Liverpool both sacked their managers, bringing in Xabi Alonso and Andoni Iraola respectively in the summer.

United and Spurs both changed manager earlier in 2026, with Michael Carrick and Roberto de Zerbi having their first pre-seasons.

Last season, Chelsea finished 10th, Liverpool as defending champions were fifth, and Spurs came 17th - with United ending up third after turning things around under Carrick.

So for all four hopes were high this was going to be a better season.

Chelsea are fifth, with only one defeat so far, and have scored 10 goals... but conceded nine - the fourth worst record in the division.

They have conceded two or more goals in each of their first four matches of a Premier League season for the first time since 2015-16.

Liverpool are down in seventh, unbeaten after four games - but three of those are draws.

It is just the third time in the last 63 seasons they have failed to win either of their first two home league games.

United are 13th with four points - equalling their worst start to a Premier League season since 1992-93... level with last season.

They have had more shots than anybody else in the league - 84 - and the second fewest shots conceded (41).

Despite that they have conceded as many as they have scored - seven.

Spurs would not have considered themselves in the title race after two 17th-placed finishes but would have hoped for a better start as they currently sit... 17th.

And even worse than that, it was the first time in the club's history they have failed to score in their first four league games.

Prior to this campaign, 80 teams in the English top-flight have won their first four league games of the season.

Of those, just 24 went on to win the title, proving that early dominance does not necessarily mean a side will last the pace.

In the Premier League era, nine of the 28 sides to win four on the bounce at the start of a season have gone on to lift the title, most recently Manchester City in 2023-24.

As the graphic below shows, there have been just six previous Premier League seasons in which two or more teams have won each of their first four fixtures.

Sports.title: Officials and lawmakers at odds over releasing VAR audio
Sports.text:
It was one of the most controversial VAR decisions in years, yet the 74,161 inside Old Trafford were kept in the dark.

When referee Michael Oliver blew his whistle to award Erling Haaland's goal, few would have had any clue the real offside situation involved Enzo Fernandez.

Viewers on television, however, were able to learn exactly what happened with the goal that gave Manchester City a 1-0 win.

It is not just about the most contentious decisions, either.

On Saturday, Crystal Palace defender Axel Disasi was sent off for serious foul play in the 3-2 loss to Ipswich Town.

The Chelsea loanee stood on the side of the pitch for over a minute while the VAR checked the red card. And those at Selhurst Park remained in the dark.

We're almost 10 years into the use of the video assistant referee, and still the match-going fan is treated like a second-class citizen.

The television commentary team are in a unique position, able to hear what the VAR is saying but not the referee.

The idea is they can pass on the context of VAR checks to the viewers, who are not permitted to make those judgements themselves.

Will football ever get to a place where fans are trusted to hear what the video official is saying, just like other sports?

When Howard Webb took over as the Premier League referees' chief in 2022, he promised greater transparency and openness.

Huge strides have been made on that front, and the Match Officials Mic'd Up VAR TV show was a trailblazer among the top European leagues.

It was a logical move from Webb, considering his time as the boss of referees in Major League Soccer prior to his move back to England.

In 2019, MLS became the first league to publicly share VAR audio after matches through a show called Inside VAR - effectively the pre-cursor to Match Officials Mic'd Up in the Premier League.

Attempts to bring audio directly into live matches has proved unsuccessful.

BBC Sport understands some leagues and the lawmakers can't find a consensus.

Webb has been part of a working group set up to lobby to get the rules relaxed, to eventually enable the audio to be played live.

But the Ifab, who are football's lawmakers, and in particular Fifa, are not close to being on board with fully pulling back the curtain.

Discussions about changing the regulations regularly stall, with concerns about the quality of communications worldwide, added pressure on officials during reviews and that the credibility of referees could be affected.

Part of the reason is that so many decisions are subjective and open to interpretation. It is possible for someone to disagree with almost any call that is made.

In an interview three years ago, Lukus Brud, the Ifab secretary and chief executive, told BBC Sport that allowing the audio to be played live would be "chaotic" due to the number of people speaking.

Webb is in a unique position as being the only referees' chief to experiment with live VAR broadcast.

In August 2020, during the MLS is Back Tournament following the Covid shutdown, the league became the only competition to ever broadcast live VAR audio during matches.

It was considered a success, but six years on from that short experiment there have been no further experiments anywhere.

Rather than MLS providing a blueprint for the game to move forward, it proved nothing more that a footnote for VAR.

Webb, of course, can also only go as fast as the Premier League wants to go because refereeing body Pro Ref does not make any unilateral decisions like this.

While the Premier League has been innovative in some ways, in others it has been overtaken by other major leagues.

English football has innovated with RefCam with live audio this season, and publishing the transcript of the discussions between the VAR and the referee.

And the league was one of the first to have its referees announce VAR decisions - a rare win for the match-going fan over those sat at home.

But there has been limited progress with Match Officials Mic'd Up, which is still only monthly.

Fortunately, the first edition this season airs on Tuesday, providing the perfect opportunity to play out the audio of the Fernandez offside decision.

Yet other contentious incidents, like the Harry Maguire handball before Manchester United scored against Ipswich, or the failure to award a penalty to Arsenal at Aston Villa, happened weeks ago with no audio made available.

This is where the Premier League can improve.

Take the Spanish La Liga, which publishes the VAR audio and video of every subjective intervention, external - when the referee has visited the monitor to change their decision - across social media a few hours after the match has finished. Not weeks later.

Yet the Italian Serie A has gone in the other direction, cancelling Open VAR - its version of Match Officials Mic'd Up - at the end of last season due to the pressure it placed upon its officials.

The German Bundesliga does not have a VAR show - though this may change in the coming seasons - and only shares audio clips when relevant.

If the VAR audio was to be made available live, which seems a long way off, there would still be limitations.

The fact is that the majority of checks take place when a game is on-going, and as such it would be unrealistic to think commentators would just stop speaking. Nor would fans want that.

But many others happen, such as the City goal, when the game is stopped. So why not share this?

One issue is that the VAR will start working on a check or review immediately, so a broadcaster switching to this feed might do so late and lose the context.

VAR delays are bad enough without waiting for a TV producer to give you the nod to start work.

But there could be ways around that.

The more likely scenario is that the VAR audio would only be played live when a referee is at the pitchside monitor. That would allow a more formulaic approach, pretty much like cricket's live DRS reviews.

In the Australian A League, when at the monitor the big screens in the ground show live exactly what the referee is watching. Though again, no audio.

That would still fall far short of what fans really want. There would be no audio of Sunday's contentious incidents.

Football has always been so far behind other sports when it comes to using technology.

The wheels of progress have turned slowly, and there appears to be little appetite to change that when it comes to the VAR audio.

Sports.title: Arsenal to contact Pro Ref over Ezri Konsa penalty incident
Sports.text:
Arsenal will contact refereeing body Pro Ref over the incident in which Ezri Konsa conceded a penalty in Saturday's win over Sunderland.

Konsa and Black Cats defender Dan Ballard were involved in a physical exchange inside the penalty area in which the Arsenal defender was adjudged to have fouled the Sunderland player for excessive holding.

After the game Gunners manager Mikel Arteta criticised the decision, and it is understood the Premier League champions will hold talks with the professional referee's body for an explanation as to why the penalty was awarded.

It is understood Arsenal are keen to avoid major refereeing decisions impacting on results and want clarity over how referee John Brooks came to his decision.

Brooks initially awarded Sunderland the spot-kick on the field, and the decision was backed up by the video assistant referee (VAR).

"The referee's call of penalty to Sunderland for a holding offence by Konsa on Ballard was checked and confirmed by VAR," read a statement published by the Premier League Match Centre.

But after the game Arteta said: "This is not acceptable at this level.

"I watched it 20 times and I cannot find a way to understand how they think to give a penalty in that situation, or the way the VAR has to intervene.

"So I don't know what to think. I'm sad that we have to discuss this after such a beautiful game, that at this level has the gravity of that. Because that changes the course of the season and it can cost you the championship.

"At this level, with all the work we put in, this cannot happen."

Match of the Day pundits Ashley Williams and Thomas Frank both said Sunderland should not have been awarded a penalty, claiming that Arsenal should have had a free-kick.

"I think he's got it completely wrong," said Williams. "It's almost like a perfect hip toss in judo [from Ballard]. In no way is it a penalty."

Sports.title: Ludek Miklosko obituary: West Ham goalkeeper whose fans still chant his name
Sports.text:
More than a quarter of a century after he stopped playing for West Ham, the chant still regularly sung by fans shows the affection in which former Hammers goalkeeper Ludek Miklosko is held.

My name is Ludo Miklosko,

I come from near Moscow,

I play in goal for West Ham (West Ham!),

When I walk down the street,

Everyone that I meet,

Says "Oi! Big boy! What's your name?"

Miklosko announced late in 2024 that he was withdrawing from further cancer treatment three years after his diagnosis. Days later he returned to West Ham for a Premier League match against Liverpool to a hero's reception.

On Monday, it was announced he had died at the age of 64.

No matter that his birthplace of Prostejov is about 1,000 miles from Moscow (and actually nearer London), Miklosko was a popular player who went on a trailblazing journey and won 42 international caps - the last two for the Czech Republic following Czechoslovakia's dissolution.

In a pre-internet era, Miklosko was barely known outside his homeland when he arrived in the English capital from Czech club Banik Ostrava in February 1990 as a long-term replacement for Phil Parkes in West Ham's goal.

The fall of communism had opened a path for players to leave eastern Europe for the elite leagues in the west, and after a two-month wait for a work permit during which he trained alone, he eventually became the first footballer to move from Czechoslovakia to England.

Manager Lou Macari travelled to Prague to accompany his £300,000 signing on the flight to Heathrow Airport but missed his debut, resigning a day later, with Billy Bonds taking over.

Miklosko, then aged 28, began his time in England staying in a hotel, with little grasp of English and no car, and would be given lifts to and from training by team-mates Ian Bishop and Trevor Morley.

The goalkeeper went on to become a cult figure with supporters, making 374 appearances for the Hammers over eight years, and had a spell back at the club as goalkeeping coach after ending his playing days with a three-year stint at Queens Park Rangers.

He was named the Hammer of the Year as West Ham won promotion back to the top flight in 1991 with a squad that included Julian Dicks and Frank McAvennie, and appeared in FA Cup and League Cup semi-finals.

The 6ft 5in shot-stopper will be particularly remembered for some brilliant displays in front of the old Boleyn Ground crowd.

Most memorable of all was on the final day of the 1994-95 season, when he single-handedly kept out the attacking might of Manchester United to deny them a third consecutive Premier League title.

A victory for the visitors would have given them the trophy as Blackburn lost to Liverpool, but they were held to a 1-1 draw and Rovers were crowned champions.

Miklosko stood in United's way, denying Mark Hughes, Lee Sharpe and Andy Cole in what frustrated Red Devils manager Alex Ferguson described as a "siege".

Years later, the keeper visited Manchester United's training academy, where staff recalled his efforts.

"A few of them said: 'I was there and remember that game and I hated you'. We had a good laugh about it," he told West Ham's website in 2020, saying he "never tired" of talking about that match.

Miklosko had an operation to remove a lump he discovered on his hip in 2021, and while radiotherapy initially helped with a further stomach tumour, he decided against chemotherapy for more tumours after discussions with his doctors.

He had returned to Banik Ostrava as sporting director in 2022 and wanted to carry on working. Supporters there unveiled a giant banner in support of him at a game earlier in 2025, with his picture and the words 'Big Ludo'.

"I have two football clubs in my heart - Banik Ostrava and West Ham United - and in a funny way they are very similar. Even the mentality of the fans, very similar. Hard-working people, loyal and passionate," he said,

"If I am ever doing an interview here in the Czech Republic, I am always saying this and making this comparison.

"West Ham United is my second family. After all these years, they still remember me, still sing my name, and that is a great feeling."

His name is Ludek Miklosko. He will be fondly remembered.

Sports.title: Brendon McCullum wants Kevin Pietersen to challenge methods in England role
Sports.text:
England white-ball head coach Brendon McCullum says he wants newly appointed mentor Kevin Pietersen to challenge his methods.

Pietersen criticised England players during the tour of India last year, saying none could say they "did everything they can to try and help England win".

Former batter Pietersen has joined the limited-overs set-up as a specialist mentor until next autumn's 50-over World Cup in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia.

"That [Pietersen's comments] was one of the first things we talked about," McCullum told BBC Sport.

"He said 'gee, I was just criticising you not long ago'.

"I said I don't care about that. Some of it's fair and some of it would need some explanation, but I have no problem with that.

"It's healthy when you create an environment where you're able to challenge.

"That's one thing I want him to do. It's not just bury himself in the batting per se, but look across the entire environment, look across how we run things and what we do, and if there's anything you pick up then just come and challenge me on it.

"Him and I get on well. We had natural respect playing against each other and we spent a bit of time together in the last little while, and I'm super excited to have him as part of our support staff as well."

Pietersen joined up with the squad on Sunday before the first of three T20s and three ODIs against Sri Lanka in Southampton on Tuesday.

McCullum said Pietersen was "shocked" when he first called him about "helping us challenge for a World Cup".

The pair had conversations to reach an agreement and McCullum said Pietersen was "unbelievably enthusiastic" about the prospect.

"The energy he's brought to the group already has been immense and you know I feel very privileged for us to be able to have him as a resource within our dressing room," said McCullum.

"He was obviously a brilliant cricketer. He viewed the game quite differently. He was a winner and he was a guy who left no stone unturned when it came to his preparation.

"A lot of these guys grew up watching Kev play and idolised him.

"As a coach, you're trying to provide these guys with the best environment so that they can try and achieve what they want. Adding Kev is certainly that."

England will hand a debut to Derbyshire opener Aneurin Donald in the first T20, with Phil Salt missing through injury.

Donald, who was born in Wales, has impressed in the T20 Blast and The Hundred with Trent Rockets this year and has the highest strike-rate - 232 - of any batter to have faced at least 50 balls in T20s this year.

Pace bowler Jofra Archer is rested after playing all three Tests against Pakistan, but Josh Tongue is included.

England team to face Sri Lanka in first T20: Aneurin Donald, Jos Buttler, Harry Brook (capt), Tom Banton, Jordan Cox, Will Jacks, Jamie Overton, Liam Dawson, Josh Tongue, Sonny Baker, Adil Rashid.

McCullum's sole responsibility is now for the white-ball side after he was sacked as Test coach following the series defeat by New Zealand in June.

England have appointed fellow New Zealander Stephen Fleming to the role.

The pair must juggle the workloads of England's players as they bid to regain the Ashes from Australia next summer before the World Cup.

"We've already been chatting around how we're going to try and manage some of the workloads of players and make sure we still get our best players available for the big series," said McCullum.

"We'll sit down in the coming days and map out a bit of a pathway for a few guys, but naturally guys can't play all year round.

"You're going to have to work out times that you can take them out of the physical duties of international cricket, freshen up, and then other times that you have them all ready to go.

"They will be easy conversations between two good mates with the motivation of what's right for English cricket."

The end of McCullum's reign as Test coach was tainted by off-field issues in Australia during the Ashes, while captain Ben Stokes and seamer Gus Atkinson missed the second Test against New Zealand in June after an incident in a London nightclub.

Since McCullum's departure seamer Brydon Carse has been involved in a nightclub incident while celebrating a victory for Durham.

Test captain Joe Root said he was "hacked off" and had had a "very strong discussion" in the changing room.

McCullum said he is in "total agreement" with Root and that he wants his white-ball side to be the "fittest, strongest, most dynamic, most robust cricket team in the world".

"There is a lot of talent which sits within English cricket and if people aren't prepared to make those sacrifices and to commit to what you're trying to achieve on the field, then other guys will be given those opportunities," said McCullum.

"It's important for Carsey now to just get his house in order and then work his way back towards banging down the door to play for England, because he's still got a long runway in front of him in terms of his career."
