EntertainmentTab.title: Pontypool-born actor Luke Evans survived Hollywood by listening to actors he admired
EntertainmentTab.text:
Actor Luke Evans said he has survived Hollywood by "watching and listening" to actors he admired.

Pontypool-born Evans made the observation while discussing his similarities and "emotional connection" to his character in a new ITV drama, The Party.

It will see Evans star as Martin Gilmour, a journalist shaped by his lifelong friendship with a wealthy and charismatic politician played by Aberystwyth-born Tom Cullen.

The stars have been seen filming at multiple locations, including a park and bars in Cardiff and Rhondda Cynon Taf, since October.

The thriller moves between the birthday party of Cullen's character, Ben Fitzmaurice, and a police investigation that follows.

Evans, who is also an executive producer of the five-part series, said he drew on his own experiences to play the character.

"I think that's probably why I resonated with the story when I read the book," Evans said of the novel the series, which is based the book written by Elizabeth Day.

"Watching and listening is how I've managed to survive this industry.

"If I'm on a film set, I'm always watching other actors or older actors that I've been admiring for years," he added.

Evans said this trait of watching others was something he shared with Gilmour, who he said he connected with on a "very deep level".

"It's not always possible when you play a role that you can pull on your own personal life or experiences.

"In this role I definitely could, even when Martin chooses completely different life choices to ones I would make in his position," he said.

EntertainmentTab.title: Critics celebrate Céline Dion's 'risky' comeback show in Paris
EntertainmentTab.text:
Iconic Canadian pop singer Céline Dion has kicked off her long-awaited comeback show in Paris on Saturday, after a six-year hiatus due to health issues.

The 58-year-old superstar was diagnosed with a rare neurological disorder called stiff person syndrome in 2022, which forced her to pull back from touring.

Dion, one of the best-selling musical artists of all time, has not performed a full show since a 2020 concert in New Jersey - the last before the Covid pandemic cut her tour short. In 2024, she performed just one song at the Paris Olympics closing ceremony.

Saturday marked the first of Dion's 26-show residency at the Paris La Défense Arena, Europe's largest covered concert arena.

"I made a promise," she told the Paris audience of about 30,000 people in her emotional return.

"I made a promise to come back, to be back on stage. And here I am. Singing for you, and singing for me," she said.

"I am everything I am because you loved me," she told the crowd.

She also broke down in tears after finishing a song, telling the audience: "I had promised myself not to cry."

"But I'm so happy to see you all. I missed you."

They weren't the only tears of the night, as the star appeared to be overcome with emotion several times.

Dion will be performing in Paris throughout September and October and into the New Year.

The Mirror's Lucy Needham, external noted that the singer was 50 minutes late to start, and may have needed extra time to "compose herself" for the "emotionally charged return".

"Eyes-brimming, the veteran singer gave herself little nods of approval after every line, before finally breaking down at the end of the track, seemingly overwhelmed at having made it through."

After beginning her set in a black gown, she later changed into a trouser suit "to show off some of those signature kooky dance moves," says Needham, adding that she appeared "to be having the time of her life, gyrating and slapping her thighs with glee".

The night was a "a tense, tearful, joyous affair probably even more so for the singer than for her loyal audience," writes The Telegraph's Neil McCormick, external.

She started out slow, he says. "Her voice sounded fragile and exposed, but at least it was her distinctive voice, not some autotuned approximation."

"At first, she was clearly struggling to hold herself together," he continues. "Her vocals wobbled dangerously, as if about to crack or collapse. But she was gaining confidence with every moment back on stage."

She broke down in tears as the audience roared in approval after the first song, and addressed the crowd in both French and English during the set.

"This was a high-stakes, high-wire return, perhaps the riskiest comeback in the history of showbusiness," McCormick continues, referring to her health condition.

But he concludes: "I honestly think I prefer this less superhuman Céline. Her voice is still great, but a bit more raw and real, with a rougher tone, less smoothness in the runs and more edge to her whoops and shrieks."

Sarah Leavitt, reporting from Paris for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC), external, said the crowd "was left without words" by the stunning performance.

She noted that she didn't want to cry, but "of course she cried right away."

Dion also "endeared herself" to the crowd by saying during one song that she wanted to stop and start over.

Will Hodgkinson at the Times of London, external writes in his review, "miraculously, her art will go on," that the performance was "overwhelming".

She "looked suitably humbled and tearful" as she emerged, he said, going on to praise the stage direction.

"Truly, she was throwing the love at the crowd, who threw it right back at her. There was no holding back. It was quite overwhelming, actually," he writes.

The performance was "complete with both costume, key change and air of tragic, important romance".

"Céline Dion's strength lies in being a diva with the common touch while being as French as they get, even if she is Canadian. She fulfilled that role with all the verve you could hope for," writes Hodgkinson.

"The concert had a spiritual feel, with visual interludes steeped in biblical imagery alluding to a pilgrimage," Elsa Keslassy writes for Variety., external

In video clips, Dion is seen wandering in a desert. "The set design was highly cinematic, with a monumental staircase sweeping up one side and a moon dominating the stage, while the backdrop appeared to have a stark, almost brutalist gray texture."

The star, known for power ballads like My Heart Will Go On and Because You Loved Me, has said she will not let her diagnosis control her life.

"The way I see it, I have two choices. Either I train like an athlete and work super hard, or I switch off and it's over," she told French Vogue magazine, external in 2024.

"I've chosen to work with all my body and soul, from head to toe, with a medical team."

When Dion announced the first leg of her Paris residency back in March, nine million fans signed up for early access tickets to the concerts, French outlet FRI reported.

The shows sold out so fast that her management company soon announced an additional 10 shows scheduled for May 2027, which have also since sold out.

Fans who were unable to snag tickets to one of the highly anticipated shows have not been left out entirely - events honouring Dion's comeback have dominated Paris in recent weeks.

Céline Dion tribute boat cruises on Seine - complete with costume contests, sing-alongs, DJ sets, are happening throughout September.

Ahead of Saturday's show, fans gathered outside Dion's Paris hotel, LeRoyal Monceau, as early as 06:00 local time to catch a glimpse of the star.

Paris City Hall organised a massive karaoke event on Friday night, attended by thousands, to celebrate Dion's return to the stage.

"I couldn't get tickets to the concert. I'm still keeping my fingers crossed and hoping, but I thought to myself: at least I can share a moment here with all the fans," Rania, a participant at the event, told Reuters.

Earlier this week, thousands of fans also gathered at a historic theatre in central Paris for two nights of karaoke and activities inspired by Dion's music.

And Paris venues and night clubs are hosting Dion-themed events around the city on Saturday night for fans who couldn't get tickets to the actual show.

EntertainmentTab.title: 'Forget Notting Hill - we set our new romcom in the east end of Glasgow'
EntertainmentTab.text:
Film fans have had plenty of chances to spot Glasgow on the big screen in recent years, from superhero blockbusters to futuristic sci-fi thrillers.

Now the city is to star in cinemas once again - but the difference is that it won't be doubling for another location. It is actually set in the city.

Romantic comedy Premature is out in cinemas next Friday, despite a microscopic budget that is the fraction of Hollywood productions like Spider-Man: Brand New Day.

The indie film - by writer and director Kevin Walls - was shot across the city, meaning landmarks such as Kelvingrove Art Gallery pop up - a well as the less obvious location of an east end flat.

The film stars James Rottger and Elle Watson as Cameron and Eilidh - mismatched flatmates who face the prospect of parenthood after a one-night stand.

"We shot quite a bit in a flat in the east end, maybe about nine days there," Walls said.

"There is a key scene we did in a close there. It is not necessarily the most romantic location you would think of for a romcom, but in real life that's exactly where these things happen.

"Why can't we set a romcom in a flat in the east end? It looks really beautiful on the big screen."

That vibe is something the film's leading lady agrees with, despite Glasgow's film appearances often being due to it looking Gothic.

"We are so used to Glasgow being this dark and gritty place, but that's not reflective of the city overall", Watson said.

"It's great having it on screen as a bright and funny place, with people falling in love there. Shooting in locations I've grown up around was great too, as I've been going to Kelvingrove since I was a little kid.

"Part of me wanted to run around the building when it was all quiet. But when you see it on the screen it looks beautiful. Being from Glasgow you are so used to it that you almost become immune to the spectacle of the building, and how grand it is."

Walls admitted to BBC Scotland News that some of the choices were made through necessity.

"The locations were tricky because we didn't have any money," she said. "So we were begging – I'd usually go down and speak to people about what I was trying to do. I explained I wasn't going to tear up their space or anything like that."

Premature is the first feature film Kevin has directed, having worked on short films and adverts in the past.

He has also juggled other jobs, including lecturing and editing highlights of football matches for YouTube channels, with money raised going back into Premature.

A Kickstarter campaign helped secure funding needed for a cinema release.

"Cinema-going is really important to me, and through sheer determination I was going to get this on a cinema screen too, as it deserves to be seen there", Walls said.

Watson's character Eilidh harbours dreams of being an artist, but is frustrated that life is not going to plan. Her flatmate Cameron is meticulous and career driven, but everything changes for both of them when they drunkenly sleep together.

"This whole film is about two people being chucked out of any sense of control they thought they had," said James Rottger, who plays the leading man.

"Particularly for Cameron, that's the point of the film – I leaned into the bit of me that's a control freak and likes to do things a certain way, and then brought that out in the character."

Like his co-star, he was delighted to see so much of Glasgow on screen, and being presented in a bright light.

"It's brilliant big productions are coming here and using Glasgow as a double, but it's important we see Scotland on the big screen as itself," he said.

"The film Kevin has written shows Glasgow in a warm light, literally and figuratively. The red sandstone flats, Kelvingrove, the pubs – it's all there."

For Watson, the relatability came in a different way.

"Any woman in her late 20s or 30s will have thought about children, it's omnipresent," she said.

"You feel you need to be confident about your choice as it will soon be taken away from you as you get older.

"But it was important the film is not just about Eilidh being pregnant – it's using that for her to discover who she is and what she wants from life."

Walls admits he had to overcome his own doubts during the creative process, having put so much effort in.

"There were so many times you'd think 'what am I doing here, this is a terrible idea and won't work' – I had to push past that and be confident," he said.

Seeing the finished product in cinemas will make it all worth it though, as Watson sums up.

"It feels like a miracle for this film with a tiny budget and a hope and a prayer, to be on the big screen."

EntertainmentTab.title: Drag Race co-creator Fenton Bailey speaks out after BBC axe
EntertainmentTab.text:
The executive producer of Drag Race has said there is a "crisis of representation" on TV, following the BBC's decision to axe the UK edition of the show.

Speaking exclusively to BBC News, Fenton Bailey said he did not believe there was a "hidden agenda" behind the decision, but feared "vulnerable communities are going to be even more vulnerable".

The move led viewers to raise concerns about the corporation's on-screen representation, after it also cancelled two LGBTQ+ dating shows.

A spokesperson for the BBC said the decision was down to "significant financial pressures", as it attempts to make £500m of savings.

Other shows being cancelled include Celebrity Mastermind, Blankety Blank and Live at the Apollo, and more than 500 job losses have also been announced.

World of Wonder (WOW) announced future series of Drag Race UK, including a new All Stars version, will be broadcast exclusively on the company's own streamer, WOW Presents Plus.

BBC News spoke to Bailey, screenwriters, TV critics and former Drag Race contestants about the move and what it means for on-screen representation.

When Drag Race UK launched in 2019, co-creator Fenton Bailey, who was born in Portsmouth but now lives in Los Angeles, said working with the national broadcaster felt like a "very special homecoming" for his production company, WOW.

The US version of the show, created by RuPaul Charles and produced by WOW, had been on air for more than 10 years and was a runaway success, with dozens of Emmy awards and an international following.

Fans were eagerly awaiting a UK series to showcase the unique British style of drag. Now, eight series and three spin-offs later, the programme will stop broadcasting on the BBC after the current series ends.

"Even at the best of times, queer culture is vulnerable and you can't take anything for granted," Bailey told BBC News. "Just because a door opened yesterday doesn't mean it won't be slammed shut the next."

BBC News understands discussions to renew the BBC's deal with the show lasted months, with producers hopeful an agreement could be reached, but talks ultimately failed due to the scale of the savings the corporation is trying to make.

Bailey said it was a sign of the "horrible financial situations" broadcasters are currently facing.

"The team at the BBC are amazing and so passionate about the show, this is not an easy thing for any of the people I interacted with, or something they wanted to do," he added.

Drag Race UK was consistently one of BBC Three's most popular offerings, but according to Barb Audiences data, while average viewing figures for the series rose between 2022 and 2024, overall they've fallen around 15% over the past four years, against a backdrop of declining TV viewing figures across the board.

Bailey said the figures "haven't plummeted," but had instead fallen in line with other terrestrial TV shows, and said the number of viewers watching on social media had risen "because that's where the audience has gone."

Following the announcement, some viewers speculated the show could be acquired by another UK broadcaster, but Bailey suggested the show's creators may prefer to go it alone.

"We love partnerships, but in this particular moment, having the freedom to make the show the way we want may be preferable to getting into bed with another broadcaster and potentially be in the same situation a few more seasons down the road."

A BBC spokesperson said: "As the BBC continues to navigate significant financial pressures and deliver the savings required of us, we have had to make some very difficult choices, none of which have been taken lightly."

Scott Bryan, TV critic and author of Out Now: A Queer Journey Through Modern Television, says the move is indicative of just how severe the financial pressures facing broadcasters have become.

"I can imagine Drag Race is an expensive show to make," Bryan told the BBC, "I can see the pressures the BBC are under, but it's rather concerning in regards to queer storytelling.

"You see LGBTQ+ lives reflected on soaps and primetime dramas much more casually, but there still needs to be shows specifically catering to a queer audience, and it feels like very quickly the drawbridge is pulling up."

Earlier this year the BBC announced LGBTQ+ dating shows I Kissed a Boy and I Kissed a Girl were also being cancelled. The corporation said at the time that it was "exceptionally proud" of the shows, but they had to make "difficult choices in light of our funding challenges".

Author and screenwriter Juno Dawson says viewers have begun to notice a "pattern".

She said: "I think that's why perhaps eyebrows have been raised, because Drag Race hasn't been cancelled in isolation. A couple of other LGBTQ+ shows have gone as well.

"It's a shame this is happening at the BBC, because commercial channels don't necessarily have an obligation to represent all the communities in the UK, but the BBC does and it's supposed to represent all of us, including LGBTQ+ people."

The BBC recently announced Smoggie Queens, which features predominantly LGBTQ+ characters, would be renewed for a third series, and it represents the community elsewhere through storylines in shows including Mr Loverman, Amandaland, Vigil and EastEnders.

A recent report from GLAAD, an American advocacy organisation, found film representation had fallen for a third consecutive year, external and more than 200 LGBTQ+ TV characters would disappear from screens in 2026 because of cancellations, endings or limited-run series.

While similar figures for the UK aren't collated, Dawson fears a shrinking television industry in the UK will make it harder for commissioners to make LGBTQ+ stories.

"So many of my personal shows have gotten right up to green light, but for lots of different reasons, different commissioners - not just at the BBC - have decided to back away.

"Nobody is ever going to say to you 'it's because it was too niche', but all I can keep doing is writing television that feels true to me and represents me and my life."

"It's great the show is going to carry on and shine a spotlight on the amazing drag artistry the UK has to offer," they said, "but I do mourn the possibility of someone maybe just flicking through the channels and randomly finding it."

Butch told BBC News that the show coming off the BBC may also bring some positive changes to the programme - including the possibility of prize money and sponsorships.

"It's a lot of effort to go on Drag Race, a lot of investment and emotional labour," they added, "so I hope the audience follows and keeps supporting the queens."

Fenton Bailey says he's excited about the show's future on its own streaming platform.

"We may not have the resources that the BBC has, but the spirit of Drag and RuPaul's Drag Race is about making something out of nothing," he told the BBC.

"As a community we can survive and thrive in less than optimal conditions.

"We have. We can. We will."

EntertainmentTab.title: Tom Felton: I'm so excited to see Rupert Grint play Ron Weasley again
EntertainmentTab.text:
Every night on Broadway, Tom Felton walks on stage to a roar from the audience. He had expected the reaction to die down after the first week, but it never did.

Almost 15 years after his final appearance as Draco Malfoy on screen, Felton has spent the past 10 months playing the character again in the Broadway production of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child.

I meet the actor in a dressing room at NBC Studios, just off Times Square in New York. He's just finished a live television appearance and in a few hours will be back on stage for his next performance.

He greets me with a hug and says he is excited to speak to BBC News because his mum and 100-year-old grandfather will see it. His family are some of his biggest supporters - his mum has seen the show five times already, while his dad is due to visit next month.

That support mirrors the enthusiasm Felton has encountered from Harry Potter fans, which he says still surprises him more than two decades after he first played Draco.

"I thought the applause would stop in the first week and it has not.

"It's very humbling and lovely to know how much the characters still mean to people now and if it brings them to the theatre, that's the best."

He is also struck by how many of the fans now approaching him were not alive when the first Harry Potter film was released.

"There are fans that approach me shouting 'Draco' who weren't even born when I was in the first film," he says.

Felton was the first of the original Harry Potter cast to reprise his role in the theatre show, but he will not be the only one for much longer, as Rupert Grint is set to return as Ron Weasley on Broadway in February.

The 38-year-old actor says he called his former co-star as soon as he heard the news.

"We are typically - and he will agree with me - pretty bad at our phone game, but when I heard the news I called him immediately and I'm so excited for him," Felton says. "Who doesn't want to see Rupert Grint play Ron Weasley again? Come on!"

I ask whether Felton offered any advice to his co-star but he laughs and says absolutely not, pointing out that Grint has already appeared on Broadway.

"I don't think he needs any advice from me. If anything, I would be taking it from him."

He adds that Grint has a "Ron Weasley laissez-faire approach to these things".

More than two decades after they first met on the Harry Potter set, Felton says the friendships between the young cast have endured.

He describes Grint, Daniel Radcliffe and Emma Watson as "best mates" and "family", even if getting them all in the same place is now difficult.

"We are usually in four different corners of the Earth, so it's hard to get together," he says, adding that their support since his return to Draco has been "fantastic".

As Felton and Grint return to familiar roles on stage, a new generation is preparing to take over the characters in HBO's television adaptation of the books set to air later this year.

Felton recently met his successor, Lox Pratt, and "saw a lot of myself in him".

Felton says he was struck by Pratt's confidence and describes him as a "charming young man and fabulous actor".

Their families have even been in touch.

"My mum is in contact with his mum and I'm encouraging him to be as cheeky as possible - but professional first."

Felton says he is not worried about the level of scrutiny Pratt and the other young actors may face as they take on some of the best-known characters in popular culture.

"You just enjoy it for what it is.

"I'm not worried about that at all for him. He's got a very good head on his shoulders and what you don't know doesn't hurt you. I'm sure he's not one to scroll through negative comments."

Nor does Felton appear concerned that Harry Potter is being adapted again relatively soon after the films.

Instead, he says the longer television format offers the chance to explore parts of the books that the films did not have time for.

"We had two hours to fit in a lot of content and the wizarding world is vast, so it's exciting to know they can dive in deeper."

"I hope the fans of the books and films explore more about Draco," he says.

While some actors might want to distance themselves from the role that made them famous, Felton has embraced his connection to Harry Potter.

He says the franchise has given him "a life I could never have imagined" and that, even today, it is "bringing people together from every corner of the earth".

Asked whether this really is the last time he will play Draco, Felton is reluctant to rule anything out.

"I suppose I said 15 years ago that was the end of Draco and I was leaving him forever, but here I am.

"It's hard to say with any certainty what's to come."

EntertainmentTab.title: Catherine Zeta-Jones says term 'nepo baby' is horrific
EntertainmentTab.text:
Hollywood star Catherine Zeta-Jones has declared the phrase "nepo baby" is "horrific".

The Mumbles-born actor told The Sunday Times: "These kids didn't ask to be born into this."

The term nepo baby refers to children of famous parents perceived to have achieved riches and success off their parents' backs.

The 56-year-old is married to Kirk Douglas' son, Michael Douglas, and they have two children - Dylan and Carys - who have both followed their parents into showbiz.

Dylan, she said, was pursuing acting while Carys was interested in directing. She insisted her children were "plugging away".

"You have to go with your dreams, your passion," Zeta-Jones said.

"It's hard for them to forge a way forward on their own.

"This horrific phrase 'nepo baby' is horrible because these kids didn't ask to be born into this, they're finding their own way in life.

"But they love it, and they're good.

"Otherwise, Michael and I would be the first to go, 'you know what? Maybe law school looks really good'."

Zeta-Jones' big break came when she landed a West End role in 42nd Street in 1987, becoming a household name in the UK in 1991 when she starred in ITV hit The Darling Buds Of May with Only Fools and Horses legend David Jason.

She has since become a global superstar, with roles in The Mask Of Zorro, Entrapment, Traffic and 2002's adaptation of Chicago.

"I had a sniff of the joy of being in the theatre so young," she said.

"I went, 'I want to do this. I can't imagine going through school and A-Levels in Swansea.'"

Zeta-Jones met Romancing The Stone star Douglas, 81, at France's Deauville Film Festival, in August 1998.

With a 25-year age gap between them, they were engaged a year later, marrying at The Plaza hotel in New York in 2000.

Dylan was born in 2000 and Carys in 2003.

EntertainmentTab.title: Oscar-winning film producer Jeremy Thomas dies aged 77
EntertainmentTab.text:
Oscar-winning producer Jeremy Thomas, whose films included The Last Emperor and Sexy Beast, has died aged 77.

The British filmmaker "passed away peacefully" surrounded by family and loved ones at his home in Oxfordshire on Friday, his publicist said in a statement.

Thomas built an international reputation over a career spanning five decades, working with directors including David Cronenberg, Nagisa Oshima, Julien Temple and Nicolas Roeg and backing independent films alongside mainstream successes.

His best known film, Bernardo Bertolucci's The Last Emperor, won nine Academy Awards, including best picture, and earned Thomas an Oscar as producer in 1988.

The critically-acclaimed biographical drama about the final monarch of China's Qing dynasty starred Joan Chen, Peter O'Toole and Vivian Wu.

Thomas repeatedly collaborated with Bertolucci, also producing The Sheltering Sky, Little Buddha, Stealing Beauty and The Dreamers.

He worked with several British directors at the start of their careers including Ben Wheatley, Jonathan Glazer, Stephen Frears and David Mackenzie.

Thomas's other credits included Oshima's Merry Christmas, Mr Lawrence - starring David Bowie - Cronenberg's A Dangerous Method, Roeg's Bad Timing and Eureka, and Matteo Garrone's Pinocchio.

He also produced Fast Food Nation, The Great Rock 'n' Roll Swindle, The Hit and adaptations of the JG Ballard books Crash and High-Rise.

After beginning as a film editor, London-based Thomas landed his first production role on the 1976 Australian film Mad Dog Morgan.

A former chairman of the British Film Institute, he won a Bafta for outstanding British contribution to cinema in 1990. Thomas received the European Film Academy's award for outstanding European achievement in world cinema in 2006 and was made a CBE in the New Year Honours in 2009.

Thomas's latest collaboration with Japanese director Takashi Miike, Bad Lieutenant:Tokyo, is due to premiere at the Toronto Film Festival on Monday.

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘A double entendre in every crevice’: what, beyond near-naked tennis, is Sydney Sweeney’s game?
EntertainmentTab.text:
Bear with me here, but I’m beginning to suspect Sydney Sweeney is a very fine actor. It’s a skill she has been recognised for in the past, of course, winning nominations for Emmys for Euphoria and The White Lotus, but I mean it in a deeper sense, related to her work in advertising rather than drama – can she do more than play a role? Can she make you feel what she’s feeling?

In her “controversial” new ad for the sports prediction site Novig (the scare quotes are because, when you’re begging for controversy this hard, you shouldn’t just be handed it on a plate), she adopts the garb of various sports. Her face, body, aspect, gait and mien are all carefully configured to amp up the erotic overtones to the maximum degree, and yet the feeling that beams out of each image is: “This is really going to piss people off, and I couldn’t be more delighted.” Her expression is so speechful that you cannot help but share in some of her hellion joy.

In brief: the proposition of the betting site is that it’s only for betting on sports – no wars, no deaths, no politics, just sports. Even the captions, absent the Sweeney, are a red rag to a bull, since betting on wars and death is a disgusting and inhumane thing to do – the surge in people trying to spin cash out of deaths in Iran, in Ukraine, says something profound about where we’ve got to in late capitalism. Whatever that profound thing is, it’s definitely not funny.

However, we are where we are, and that’s not Sweeney’s concern. She is there to wrinkle out the double entendre from every conceivable crevice. Do spherical things remind you of breasts? What if I get these two American footballs and put them in front of my actual breasts? Would it help if I was naked to the waist? Ah, better still if I were wearing no clothes at all and only the footballs stood between me and my modesty? The age-old tennis shot, immortalised by the 80s Athena poster in which the viewer is invited to consider just how nearly they can see a player’s butt – well, that’s here, only this time minus the skirt.

Sweeney’s facial expressions are like a WikiHow gallery, “how to: soft-porn” – they often feel quite old-fashioned, pert or faux naive, more like 70s graphic novel erotica than modern, up-to-the-minute pornography. Yet, throughout, there is a layer of knowingness: “I know exactly how much I’m going to drive you mad, and why.”

Truthfully, it’s hard (as a card-carrying member of the wokerati, just out here in the world, trying to keep up) to figure out what the fundamental provocation is. Sweeney famously last made headlines with the “Sydney Sweeney has great jeans” ad for American Eagle Outfitters. It was taken by many to be a call back to Donald Trump’s “You have great genes, you know that?” speech, which itself was taken as a densely layered challenge to the world, that his supporters were better human specimens than everyone else. Was the speech white supremacist or simply Trumpian-supremacist? You couldn’t really stick anything on him because, as ever, it was only atmospherically decipherable. Sweeney, however – with her very blondness, her unarguable whiteness – people did stick a white-supremacist agenda on, one she soon decried, saying she was against “divisiveness”.

Ever since, Sweeney has been taken as an anti-woke poster-girl, though since nobody can agree what “woke” means, still less what “anti-” it entails, this poster is more confusing than an avant garde typographer’s ball. She seems to want to kick that hornet’s nest with this Novig ad, but is it by inviting her own objectification? Or is there a complicated message in there about femaleness in elite sport, which has become such a lightning rod for anti-trans activism? Or are we supposed to disapprove of the pornification of the visual realm?

None of the above! Ariarne Titmus, four-time Olympic gold medal-winning swimmer, explained on Instagram: it’s “a kick in the face to every woman who had dedicated her life to perfecting her craft, but every woman who enjoys sports for what it really is – teamwork, friendship, dedication, excellence, unity”. And now she says it, yes, that makes perfect sense. What Sydney Sweeney’s game is, beyond almost-naked tennis, is anyone’s guess.

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘The eye-gouging was very, very satisfying’: how we made cave horror classic The Descent
EntertainmentTab.text:
Neil Marshall, writer/director

I was introduced to Christian Colson at Celador Films off the back of [2002 horror film] Dog Soldiers, and I pitched them a project – actually a feature-length version of my student graduation film – about zombies on an oil rig. They liked it but said it was too expensive, so on the train back to Newcastle I was asking myself what would make a really scary horror film that could be contained and so made on a budget. I was thinking of things set in the dark and was like, well … caves. At the back of my mind was a school trip to a lead mine where the guide had said, “OK, everybody, turn your lights off” and, for the first time, I experienced a darkness that I just couldn’t fathom.

We wanted the film to feel as realistic as possible: when you’re caving, the only lights you have are what you take with you. There are no beautiful shafts of light making everything look pretty. It meant having huge portions of the screen in total darkness, so only when a character turns around and shines a light you finally see what’s in the shadows.

Darkness was definitely my friend, but it did mean a lot of planning because each character had to have something they could light the scene with, even if it was just a box of matches. Sam McCurdy, the director of photography, and I discussed lighting sources that we could potentially use, and I structured the film around who had which light at which time. This gave us a lighting scheme: if you’re with the fire, it’s Sarah. If it’s a torch, it’s Juno.

There isn’t a single real cave in the whole film. It was a mixture of amazing sets by Simon Bowles, a couple of matte paintings and a miniature set built by Leigh Took – the water pouring down the waterfall wasn’t water, it’s salt.

For the crawlers, I wanted something very basic-looking, not too many lines or details. The challenge was how to make them scary but keep them human, because the notion is that these are the cavemen who stayed in the cave rather than those who left the dark and started building cabins in the open. Visually they were a hybrid of Nosferatu and Iggy Pop, but movement-wise I thought we should make them like spiders – the way they’ll stop and be perfectly still before suddenly going off at 100 miles an hour and then stopping again.

I conceptualised the film as Sarah’s descent into being this primal savage: her undergoing a rebirth in order to survive, even though you’re not sure she’s going to be able to go back to society afterwards.

Shauna Macdonald, played Sarah

This was the era of FHM, Loaded and all those lads’ mags, so I initially thought it was going to be girls looking sexy in tight spaces covered in blood and gunge. I wasn’t interested in that. When I read the script, though, it was excellent. It was about a grieving mother and I also needed to be physically strong and brave. I thought, “I have to do this part because I don’t know if I’ll be able to pull it off.”

We weren’t allowed to see the crawlers or even any pictures of them. I was the first to see one because we were shooting chronologically once we got into the caves. The others were all asking “what does it look like?!” but I didn’t really know because it was quite far away. I just knew it was grey or white and slimy, and it looked a bit like Gollum.

I think Neil was right to keep us apart, because when we were faced with them, I was being leapt at by a really scary man, basically naked, who’d been training for months and months – that really focuses the mind. When we came to fight them, they were so animalistic it was really unnerving. The actors had figured out how the crawlers’ system worked and their different characteristics. You felt like you were fighting a pack with all its dynamics, and that was pretty intimidating.

That whole sequence where Sarah goes into survival mode was great. First I had the dying scene with Alex Reid, who played Beth, just making it look really easy. It was like, “OK, Alex, you’ve had an ice pick through your neck, but it’s really important that you tell these plot points …” And she was, “Yeah, cool, no problem.” And then, of course, I cave her head in with a stone. Then I get leapt on by a child crawler. He was only like 11, bless him, and I crushed his head with my boot, which was actually me stamping on a cauliflower. Then the mother finds out, and we have this fight sequence where one mother has to kill another to survive. The eye-gouging was very, very satisfying. Then another crawler comes along and I bash his head in too. Afterwards I’m submerged in this pool of blood, which was a Jacuzzi that they’d overflowed. This amazing stunt girl had to do the run and jump, because the pool was so shallow they couldn’t insure an actor to do it. All I had to do was emerge and take the glory.

In the press, it was all about “girl power”. But we were like: “Have you seen what we do to each other?!” What was very girl power was how fiercely we actors supported each other and we continue to do that. The only way you can really show love is by turning up for your friends, and the six of us have done that repeatedly for the last 21 years or so. We’ve got a WhatsApp group and still meet regularly. I do wonder, if we’d met on a different project, would the same thing happen? Or was it the film? If you throw a group of people in a cave, maybe you all come out bonded for life.

GeneralTab.title: Andy Burnham cancels engagements after death of father
GeneralTab.text:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has cancelled official engagements on Monday and Tuesday following the death of his father Roy, who had Alzheimer's.

He had been due to host a meeting of business leaders in Downing Street on Monday, and was expected to speak at the annual trade union TUC Congress in Brighton on Tuesday.

In July, Burnham spoke about his father's condition and said it had influenced his drive to reform adult social care in England.

He had also said his father's illness was so advanced that he did not know his son had become prime minister.

Speaking to the Times newspaper, external shortly before formally taking over as prime minister, Burnham said it was "a sadness, because he would be [proud]".

He continued: "The way I look at it, it's his achievement as well. A whole family achievement, although he doesn't know it."

The prime minister later said care home staff had shown his father footage of him entering Downing Street, calling it a "wonderful" thing.

Burnham said he wanted to help "my dad and the millions like him" when setting out plans to reform adult social care.

He said he had been "overwhelmed" by the skills and professionalism of care workers supporting his father.

Burnham has described how his father, a former telephone engineer, had raised him with "laughter, love and support" alongside his mother Eileen in Culcheth, Cheshire.

In his 2024 book Look North, he wrote that neither of his parents had attended university, but could have done had they "grown up in a different time and different place".

"Their knowledge of that fact seemed to make them all the more determined that their three sons would go."

Opposition politicians have offered their condolences to Burnham and his family.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said: "No matter how old you are, or how much you try to prepare, losing your father is a profoundly painful experience.

"A part of your life that has always been there is suddenly gone forever and it can feel as though a part of you won't ever be the same again."

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said: "My heart goes out to the prime minister on the loss of his dad.

"From our conversations he sounded like a wonderful man."

Green party leader Zack Polanski said: "There are moments in life such as this sad time that transcend politics and I join the whole country in sending condolences."

GeneralTab.title: Nigel Farage says £72m donation are compliant 'with the law today'
GeneralTab.text:
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has said two big donations given to his party are "100% compliant with the law today", but was not able say whether they would be permissible if a rule change, currently being debated in Parliament, were passed.

Ministers are seeking to put a £100,000 annual cap on donations from British expats, backdated to 25 March 2026.

Farage argued the government should not retrospectively declare donations illegal and threatened to retaliate by limiting trade union donations, if elected PM.

Trade union leader Paul Nowak said there was no similarity between "care workers chipping in a few quid a year through their union and a party bought and paid for by billionaires."

Over the weekend, Reform announced that it had received two donations of £36m each from wealthy businessmen Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, who are both British but have until recently lived abroad.

Speaking to the BBC, Farage said there was "no question" their donations - the largest in British political history - were within the law "as it stands".

Asked if the two men were resident in the UK by 25 March, Farage said: "I'm not going into their particular details."

He went on to criticise the government's attempts to retrospectively declare some donations illegal, saying: "This cannot be."

"If the government was allowed to do this, you know what would happen? There would be a response the other way.

"We or the Conservatives would say 'if you're going to stop legitimate donors like this, we would say to the trade unions, you can't give money'."

Farage argued such a move would "collapse" the system of political funding and lead to taxpayers having to fund political parties, a system he said would be opposed by the British public.

Since 2020, Labour has received almost £43m from trade unions, who raise their money through individual workers' membership fees.

The House of Lords is currently debating the government's Representation of the People Bill which caps the amount British people living overseas can donate to political parties at £100,000.

The bill also states that those who moved back to the UK would have to wait for at least a year before donating more than £100,000.

The legislation states that donors must have been registered as in the UK by 25 March 2026 in order to avoid the cap.

It is not currently clear exactly when Delo and Harborne returned to the UK.

Education Minister Georgia Gould told the BBC's Today programme the government was "really worried about the big money that is coming into politics... and sometimes money from overseas that is shaping politics rather than the ordinary voters".

She said the new rule changes had been added to the bill, following a report by former senior civil servant Sir Philip Rycroft into foreign interference in British politics, published on 25 March.

The two £36m donations to Reform have reignited questions about political funding.

Speaking to Matt Chorley on Radio 5 Live, Sir Philip said examining domestic donations had not been within the remit of his review but that there was a case for capping all donations, whether they came from British citizens living in the UK or overseas.

"I don't see any reason why we should have these mega sums of money coming into British politics," he said.

He added that the government's decision to retrospectively ban certain donations was "going to be controversial" but said: "If you say, you're going to change the rules to cap donations at some point in the future, then clearly the risk is that you get a lot of those donations coming through the door before you're able to do that."

Farage said the donations would allow his party to "catch up with the other big parties" and enable them to "professionalise".

He argued that trade unions gave money to Labour so that it would enact their policies and that donors gave money to the Conservative Party in order to get "knighthoods and peerages".

By contrast he said neither Harborne or Delo would get peerages or government contracts, if Reform won the next general election.

Asked if the two men had influence over Reform's policy on cryptocurrency, Farage said he had shown them his party's paper on the subject and they both "thought it made sense".

He added that the two men "will not benefit" from Reform's policies, which he said aimed to properly regulate cryptocurrency.

Farage was speaking on the same day as the Trade Unions Congress, the federation of trade unions, held its annual conference.

TUC general secretary Nowak said Reform were a "party for sale" and their donations were "a crisis for democracy".

Sharon Graham, leader of the Unite union, said the government should go further and put a cap on individual donations made by UK residents.

Speaking on Sunday, Conservative shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat said it was important to ensure "we do not end up with a sort of Americanisation of politics where money just sort of runs free".

Liberal Democrat Cabinet Office spokeswoman Lisa Smart called for emergency legislation to cap campaign donations and spending. Similarly, the Green Party urged the Labour Party to "find its spine and support a tight cap".

GeneralTab.title: Government set to nationalise troubled steel firm, minister says
GeneralTab.text:
A plan to nationalise the UK's third-largest steelworks is being developed by the government, MPs have been told.

Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds told the House of Commons ministers were looking to acquire Speciality Steel UK (SSUK), which has sites in Stocksbridge and Rotherham in South Yorkshire and Wednesbury in the West Midlands.

The government initially took control of SSUK, previously part of Liberty Steel, last year after it was forced to liquidate by the High Court.

Reynolds said a bidder had come forward earlier this year, but the government had decided against supporting it, citing "serious concerns" over the proposed financing of the deal and "protections for UK taxpayers".

Ministers had therefore decided that the government would plan its own formal acquisition of the business, he explained.

Production at the business, which employs about 1,300 people, was paused several months ago, with staff put on furlough on reduced wages.

Reynolds told the Commons: "Having concluded that we cannot support the preferred bidder's proposal, we are faced with a choice.

"We can allow events to take their course through the liquidation process and risk being left with no say in the future of these sites, or we can act.

"We will therefore engage with the official receiver sale process and develop a proposal for the public acquisition of SSUK.

"This will preserve strategic control and ensure that all credible future opportunities can be properly considered before irreversible decisions are taken."

Future decisions and spending commitments relating to the business would be "subject to detailed due diligence and funded from existing government budgets", Reynolds said.

He added: "Working towards public acquisition will create the necessary time and space to undertake a full assessment of the opportunities available.

"It will let us consider future industrial use, regeneration opportunities and the role that specialist manufacturing capabilities could play in supporting growth and our national resilience."

In a message to workers, he said: "I will do all I can to secure a bright future for you, your communities and your families."

GeneralTab.title: Rent rises set to speed up in gloomy forecast for tenants
GeneralTab.text:
The rising cost of renting a home in the UK has accelerated after a three-year slowdown - with tenants told to expect more pain to come.

Average rental costs for new tenancies were up 2.6% in July compared with a year earlier, according to property website Zoopla.

That remains lower than the rate of rising prices in general, but the property portal has forecast annual rent rises among privately rented homes will hit 4% or 5% by the end of the year.

It said there were fewer homes available to rent and - with potential first-time buyers put off by higher mortgage rates - competition for rental places in some areas was more intense.

"Our latest report shows how sensitive the rental market is to even modest changes in how many homes are available for rent," said Richard Donnell, executive director at Zoopla.

"Growing the number of homes for rent through increased investment is the most sustainable route to boosting choice for renters and ensuring stability in rent levels over the long run."

The Renters' Rights Act came into force in England at the start of May, and was described as the biggest shake-up of the sector in more than 30 years.

Separately, the rising cost of renting has calmed recently. It fell to a low of 1.6% in February, Zoopla data shows.

But since then, the number of homes on the market for renters has been squeezed, with 3% fewer being available than a year ago.

In addition, each listing now receives an average of more than five enquiries. That is a long way short of the long queues for properties after the pandemic, but is still the most intense competition for nearly two years.

Rental demand was particularly significant in London, the Zoopla report said.

articles.title: Andy Burnham cancels engagements after death of father
articles.text:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has cancelled official engagements on Monday and Tuesday following the death of his father Roy, who had Alzheimer's.

He had been due to host a meeting of business leaders in Downing Street on Monday, and was expected to speak at the annual trade union TUC Congress in Brighton on Tuesday.

In July, Burnham spoke about his father's condition and said it had influenced his drive to reform adult social care in England.

He had also said his father's illness was so advanced that he did not know his son had become prime minister.

Speaking to the Times newspaper, external shortly before formally taking over as prime minister, Burnham said it was "a sadness, because he would be [proud]".

He continued: "The way I look at it, it's his achievement as well. A whole family achievement, although he doesn't know it."

The prime minister later said care home staff had shown his father footage of him entering Downing Street, calling it a "wonderful" thing.

Burnham said he wanted to help "my dad and the millions like him" when setting out plans to reform adult social care.

He said he had been "overwhelmed" by the skills and professionalism of care workers supporting his father.

Burnham has described how his father, a former telephone engineer, had raised him with "laughter, love and support" alongside his mother Eileen in Culcheth, Cheshire.

In his 2024 book Look North, he wrote that neither of his parents had attended university, but could have done had they "grown up in a different time and different place".

"Their knowledge of that fact seemed to make them all the more determined that their three sons would go."

Opposition politicians have offered their condolences to Burnham and his family.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said: "No matter how old you are, or how much you try to prepare, losing your father is a profoundly painful experience.

"A part of your life that has always been there is suddenly gone forever and it can feel as though a part of you won't ever be the same again."

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said: "My heart goes out to the prime minister on the loss of his dad.

"From our conversations he sounded like a wonderful man."

Green party leader Zack Polanski said: "There are moments in life such as this sad time that transcend politics and I join the whole country in sending condolences."

articles.title: Nigel Farage says £72m donation are compliant 'with the law today'
articles.text:
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has said two big donations given to his party are "100% compliant with the law today", but was not able say whether they would be permissible if a rule change, currently being debated in Parliament, were passed.

Ministers are seeking to put a £100,000 annual cap on donations from British expats, backdated to 25 March 2026.

Farage argued the government should not retrospectively declare donations illegal and threatened to retaliate by limiting trade union donations, if elected PM.

Trade union leader Paul Nowak said there was no similarity between "care workers chipping in a few quid a year through their union and a party bought and paid for by billionaires."

Over the weekend, Reform announced that it had received two donations of £36m each from wealthy businessmen Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, who are both British but have until recently lived abroad.

Speaking to the BBC, Farage said there was "no question" their donations - the largest in British political history - were within the law "as it stands".

Asked if the two men were resident in the UK by 25 March, Farage said: "I'm not going into their particular details."

He went on to criticise the government's attempts to retrospectively declare some donations illegal, saying: "This cannot be."

"If the government was allowed to do this, you know what would happen? There would be a response the other way.

"We or the Conservatives would say 'if you're going to stop legitimate donors like this, we would say to the trade unions, you can't give money'."

Farage argued such a move would "collapse" the system of political funding and lead to taxpayers having to fund political parties, a system he said would be opposed by the British public.

Since 2020, Labour has received almost £43m from trade unions, who raise their money through individual workers' membership fees.

The House of Lords is currently debating the government's Representation of the People Bill which caps the amount British people living overseas can donate to political parties at £100,000.

The bill also states that those who moved back to the UK would have to wait for at least a year before donating more than £100,000.

The legislation states that donors must have been registered as in the UK by 25 March 2026 in order to avoid the cap.

It is not currently clear exactly when Delo and Harborne returned to the UK.

Education Minister Georgia Gould told the BBC's Today programme the government was "really worried about the big money that is coming into politics... and sometimes money from overseas that is shaping politics rather than the ordinary voters".

She said the new rule changes had been added to the bill, following a report by former senior civil servant Sir Philip Rycroft into foreign interference in British politics, published on 25 March.

The two £36m donations to Reform have reignited questions about political funding.

Speaking to Matt Chorley on Radio 5 Live, Sir Philip said examining domestic donations had not been within the remit of his review but that there was a case for capping all donations, whether they came from British citizens living in the UK or overseas.

"I don't see any reason why we should have these mega sums of money coming into British politics," he said.

He added that the government's decision to retrospectively ban certain donations was "going to be controversial" but said: "If you say, you're going to change the rules to cap donations at some point in the future, then clearly the risk is that you get a lot of those donations coming through the door before you're able to do that."

Farage said the donations would allow his party to "catch up with the other big parties" and enable them to "professionalise".

He argued that trade unions gave money to Labour so that it would enact their policies and that donors gave money to the Conservative Party in order to get "knighthoods and peerages".

By contrast he said neither Harborne or Delo would get peerages or government contracts, if Reform won the next general election.

Asked if the two men had influence over Reform's policy on cryptocurrency, Farage said he had shown them his party's paper on the subject and they both "thought it made sense".

He added that the two men "will not benefit" from Reform's policies, which he said aimed to properly regulate cryptocurrency.

Farage was speaking on the same day as the Trade Unions Congress, the federation of trade unions, held its annual conference.

TUC general secretary Nowak said Reform were a "party for sale" and their donations were "a crisis for democracy".

Sharon Graham, leader of the Unite union, said the government should go further and put a cap on individual donations made by UK residents.

Speaking on Sunday, Conservative shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat said it was important to ensure "we do not end up with a sort of Americanisation of politics where money just sort of runs free".

Liberal Democrat Cabinet Office spokeswoman Lisa Smart called for emergency legislation to cap campaign donations and spending. Similarly, the Green Party urged the Labour Party to "find its spine and support a tight cap".

articles.title: Member of UK armed forces dies in road traffic incident in Ukraine
articles.text:
A member of the UK armed forces has died in a road traffic incident in Ukraine, the Ministry of Defence (MoD) has announced.

The individual's family has been informed and has "requested a period of grace before further details are released", the MoD's statement said.

The incident on Saturday was not the result of hostile action, the BBC understands.

The British government has previously acknowledged a small number of personnel in Ukraine to support Kyiv's armed forces and provide security to diplomatic staff.

It is not known which service the individual was in or what their role was.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting shared his "deepest condolences" with their loved ones, writing on social media: "This is very sad news for the family and for those grieving with them in our armed forces."

A 28-year-old paratrooper, who died while watching the testing of a new defensive capability away from the front lines in December, was the first member of the armed forces killed in Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.

On Sunday, a Russian drone hit and damaged a train in Yahodyn, near the Ukraine-Poland border - shortly after former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and top European security officials had passed through on a different train on the same line.

The UK's national security adviser Jonathan Powell was among those on board.

No casualties were reported. Russia's defence ministry said it had struck "railway infrastructure" in western Ukraine, but Ukraine's state railway company said the drone's intended target "could have been the diplomatic train".

The UK has been one of Ukraine's closest allies during the war.

Ukraine was the location of Andy Burnham's first overseas trip as prime minister in August, where he met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and promised to keep up the pressure on Russia despite Moscow's "outrageous threats".

Chairing his first meeting of the "coalition of the willing", set up by the UK and France under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer, Burnham also agreed to hand over blueprints for British-made components for Scalp missiles.

articles.title: Oasis 2027: Knebworth return confirmed as well as Manchester and Glasgow gigs
articles.text:
After weeks of posting teasers on social media and underneath the Manchester sky, Oasis have confirmed a second leg of their smash hit reunion tour for summer 2027.

The band will return to the scene of their legendary 1996 gigs at Knebworth House to play four nights at the 125,000-capacity venue in September next year.

They will also play a 11-night residency at the home of their beloved Manchester City in June, after kicking off the tour with five gigs at Glasgow's Celtic Park in May.

The announcement dropped on Monday afternoon alongside a new trailer, external and a photograph of frontmen Liam and Noel Gallagher. "Start the celebrations!", read a message on the band's social media.

"After a period of reflection, 'The Most Damaging Pop Cultural Force In Recent British History' has declared itself fit for purpose and will once again return to lift the spirits of the people.

"Come witness the fitness. It shall be a sight to behold."

Oasis will return to Slane Castle in County Meath, Ireland, for two dates in September, after performances across Europe in July and in the US in August.

The now confirmed 38-date tour marks the next phase of Oasis's comeback following their acclaimed 2025 live reunion, which made an estimated £300 million at the box office.

A new ticket registration process, similar to that used for Glastonbury Festival, has been launched in a bid to avoid the noise and confusion of last time around.

The registration period began on Monday with the announcement, on the band's website, and closes at 16:00 BST on Thursday 17 September.

In the UK, tickets will then go on on sale across Friday 25, Saturday 26 and Sunday 27 September.

The band says standard ticket prices will be fixed and range between £71.50 and £266.60.

The support act will be Richard Ashcroft once again for all dates.

Singer-songwriter Noel Gallagher recently teased the band's 2027 return - after a year off - telling TalkSport, external: "There must be something happening."

The band then posted a series of cryptic videos on their official social media channels appearing to tease gigs across the UK and Europe.

This was followed by a drone display outside the Etihad Stadium last week, pointing to Monday's announcement, as well as something similar in Rome and gig posters on the Paris Metro.

Manchester City fans the Gallaghers played a string of shows together at the Etihad Stadium in 2005, almost a decade after two famous nights at their team's old ground, Maine Road, were caught on camera for a concert film titled There and Then.

A few months after Maine Road, the band played to 250,000 fans on the grounds of Knebworth House in Hertfordshire over two nights in August 1996 - shows that are regarded as Britpop's crowning moment.

More than 4% of the UK population applied for tickets to see the Gallaghers perform, alongside the likes of the Charlatans, Manic Street Preachers, The Prodigy and Chemical Brothers.

Speaking at the premiere of a Knebworth documentary film in 2021, Noel said Oasis had had "no fear" about the magnitude of the shows, adding that if they were to do it again now they would be "petrified".

The band's 2025 comeback got off to a shaky start before an E minor chord was even strummed, with fans criticising the ticket sales process after being asked to queue for hours, with some finding themselves having to pay hundreds of pounds more than they expected.

The fiasco triggered a UK government response. Following an investigation by the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), Ticketmaster agreed to several voluntary changes, external, including telling fans 24 hours in advance if a tiered pricing system is in use and giving clearer information about ticket prices while people wait in the queue, as well as not using misleading ticket labels.

Demand and expectation were huge among fans, old and new. But the band delivered, with the BBC's review saying they hadn't sounded so good since the 1990s.

Mid-way through the world tour, Noel told TalkSport that he and his bandmates had been "blown away" by the response to their return after 16 years away.

Last week, another emotional documentary chronicling the tour - and featuring the reconciled brothers' first joint interview since their acrimonious split in 2009 - was released in UK cinemas, following its premiere in Venice.

In it, Noel confirms the band is "not a power struggle any more".

On Monday, following the announcement, he told the same radio station, external that booking part two of the comeback tour had been a no-brainer.

"We were having such a great time that, why wouldn't you?" he said, while confirming there would be no new music off the back of it.

Renewed interest in Oasis recently saw their second album (What's The Story) Morning Glory? officially overtake the biggest-selling album by their heroes The Beatles in the list of the UK's most popular albums of all-time.

And Wonderwall, from that album, became a bittersweet England World Cup anthem this summer.

Excitement for Knebworth has been growing for years - ever since it was rumoured to be on the itinerary for Oasis's 2025 tour.

Earlier this summer, it emerged that the band's promoters had applied for an events licence that would cover the Knebworth gigs.

Other big artists to have performed at the grounds of the listed country house venue include Led Zeppelin, Queen, Sir Paul McCartney, Metallica and, in 2022, Liam Gallagher as a solo act.

Oasis made history over two nights in 1996, but in 2003, Robbie Williams beat their combined attendance record by playing three consecutive nights, drawing a total crowd of 375,000 people.

That record now looks set to be broken again.

"This is history" - as Noel once put it - now repeating itself.

articles.title: Immigrants held in small outdoor cages at 'Alligator Alcatraz' in Florida, investigators find
articles.text:
Immigrants held at "Alligator Alcatraz", a now-shuttered detention centre in Florida, were kept in small metal cages for hours, according to a report from the US Department of Homeland Security's watchdog.

The Office of the Inspector General (OIG) found the use of the outdoor cages - about 18sq ft (1.67sq m) - was "unprecedented among detention facilities" and dangerous.

Investigators concluded the centre also did not comply with a number of standards for hygiene, medical care, food, health and safety.

The BBC has contacted DHS's Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Florida Governor Ron DeSantis for comment. DHS told the watchdog that state officials ran the facility.

In its response included in the investigation report, DHS officials said Florida - not the federal government - had authority over day-to-day operations at the facility.

The facility was established by the state of Florida through an executive order signed by DeSantis, but the federal government paid for operational costs.

In January, the OIG conducted a surprise inspection at the detention facility, which had become one of the most notorious immigration detention centres in the US. The OIG is an independent internal watchdog at DHS. The current inspector general was appointed by President Donald Trump during his first term.

In 2025, the detention facility was built over the course of eight days in the Everglades, a protected wetland known for its alligators. Trump once joked that immigrants held there would need to learn "how to run away" from the reptiles at the facility, which civil rights groups have decried as inhumane.

In June 2026, DeSantis said the facility would close as it was only meant to be temporary.

According to the OIG report, between July 2025 and January 2026, the facility kept 79 immigrants in the small metal enclosures, describing them as "calming areas" for people to "deescalate and have time alone". They were held there from periods ranging from minutes to nearly two hours, at least once as a disciplinary measure, OIG said.

"The use of such restrictive spaces is highly unconventional and does not align with standards for humane treatment," the report stated.

articles.title: Former top civil servant received pay-off of nearly £860,000
articles.text:
A former top civil servant received a record pay-off of nearly £860,000 after he was forced out of his job by Sir Keir Starmer, just 14 months after the then-prime minister appointed him.

Lord Wormald left his role as cabinet secretary and head of the Civil Service in February by "mutual agreement" following months of media reports suggesting Downing Street was unhappy with his performance.

The Cabinet Office's accounts, external show there was "contractual compensation" of £332,897 and "additional severance" of £526,598.

The BBC understands the size of the pay-off was partly to cover Lord Wormald's pension contributions as his removal from office essentially cut his civil service career short.

He also was compensated for a mandatory "waiting period" following his departure from government. As cabinet secretary he would have had regular access to sensitive information about national security, foreign policy and the UK economy.

His salary for the period 1 April 2025 to 13 February was between £210,000 and £215,000, according to the accounts, bringing his total for the year to more than £1m.

A Cabinet Office spokesperson said: "We do not comment on HR matters.

"The permanent secretary at the Cabinet Office received a ministerial direction from the then-prime minister to proceed with the payment to the former cabinet secretary. Their exchange of letters is a matter of public record."

The accounts state Sir Keir authorised the "special severance package" on 16 February.

A note in them also states: "The former cabinet secretary elected to take early payment of his pension.

"The majority of the total severance payment was used to ensure he could access the full value of his pension that would have been due at normal retirement age, rather than it being reduced for early payment."

The BBC has approached Lord Wormald and Sir Keir for comment.

Conservative shadow Cabinet Office minister Alex Burghart said: "Chris Wormald was just one of many civil servants and advisers fired by Keir Starmer as he tried to save his own skin.

"This payout is another appalling waste of taxpayers' money by Labour."

The UK's top civil servant sits next to the prime minister during cabinet minister meetings, which usually take place weekly in Downing Street when Parliament is sitting.

They are responsible for ensuring policy decisions are put into action and are ultimately responsible for all civil servants in Great Britain.

At the time of his appointment in December 2024, Sir Keir said Lord Wormald would be tasked with "the complete re-wiring of the British state to deliver bold and ambitious long-term reform".

As a career civil servant, some questioned whether he was the best person to reform the Civil Service.

Lord Wormald was replaced in February, making him the shortest-serving cabinet secretary in the history of the post.

The FDA Union, which represents senior civil servants, responded to his departure by criticising "anonymous briefings" against him and called his treatment "a new low for this government and its relationship with the Civil Service".

Lord Wormald was replaced by Dame Antonia Romeo.

He was later given a seat in the House of Lords in one of Sir Keir's last acts as prime minister.

Lord Wormald will be an independent crossbench peer and is scheduled to formally take his seat on Thursday.

articles.title: Westminster coming to an end, say Welsh, Scottish and Northern Irish leaders
articles.text:
The first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland have declared that "Westminster's time is coming to an end".

The nationalist leaders from Plaid Cymru, Sinn Féin and the SNP - who want their countries to leave the United Kingdom - signed an agreement on Monday which said no Westminster government had the right to "block democracy".

But while Scotland's John Swinney and Northern Ireland's Michelle O'Neill called for referendums at a joint press conference, Wales' Rhun ap Iorwerth declined to give a timetable for one in his country.

Labour and Reform accused Plaid of wanting to break up the UK.

Swinney and ap Iorwerth's governments later backed a separate agreement agreed to work together on pressing UK government on "fairness" in funding and powers.

For the first time since devolution began, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland all have first ministers who want to leave the United Kingdom.

All three met on Monday as representatives of their parties. Sinn Féin president Mary Lou McDonald also attended.

The memorandum of understanding said: "For people watching across these islands - for people watching around the world - there could be no clearer sign that Westminster's time is coming to an end.

"No Westminster government has the right to block democracy or undermine the principle that our people will decide their own future.

"We recognise that our parties have different constitutional positions and that each nation will determine its own future in its own way and in its own time."

Plaid has ruled out an independence referendum before the next Senedd election in 2030.

At the press conference, ap Iorwerth said there was a "growing recognition that Westminster is not working" and "power genuinely needs to be brought closer to people and communities".

He said the May Senedd election gave his government "a mandate for change to make Wales more confident, more prosperous and more in control of its future".

"Wales should have the power, the resources, the fair treatment we need as a nation to build the future our people deserve," he said.

SNP leader Swinney said Monday was a "pivotal moment in the constitutional journey of the United Kingdom".

He said the elections in May for each nation created a situation with first ministers who believe "their countries should decide their own future".

"That principle of self-determination is an inalienable right," he said.

He described Andy Burnham as the "last prime minister of the United Kingdom".

"Because the people of Scotland, if given the choice of independence in a referendum will take that choice."

Sinn Féin's McDonald described Monday's meeting as "historic", saying: "We have the right to referendum. We have the right to decide our future.

"We will not accept or tolerate any prime minister telling us that right is off the table."

Northern Ireland's First Minister O'Neill said all three nations were "distinctively different" and had their own priorities.

But she said the "common cause here is that Westminster does not and will never serve our people well".

O'Neill serves in a power sharing executive in Northern Ireland, where the Democratic Unionist Party's (DUP) deputy first minister Emma Little-Pengelly accused the Sinn Fein politician of attempting to "weaponise the role of first minister".

In Northern Ireland, the first and deputy first minister have identical powers.

Asked by BBC Wales to clarify what the memorandum of understanding meant for Wales, and whether it meant asking Westminster not to block a Welsh independence referendum, ap Iorwerth said it was "up to the people of Wales to decide its own future".

Pressed further, he said: "The timescale will be set by the people of Wales when they are persuaded. My job is to persuade."

The Welsh government does not have the power to hold such a referendum, but ap Iorwerth told the press conference he wanted to see that devolved.

Later on Monday, Swinney and ap Iorwerth signed an agreement between the Welsh and Scottish governments.

The agreement, which is not legally binding, said it would "press the case for greater fairness for Wales and Scotland in areas such as the operation of the UK funding arrangements and powers over our constitutional future".

It said the two governments would work together on a range of issues, including tackling child poverty and maximising the benefits of their relationships with the European Union.

At a second press conference, Swinney declined to offer support for reform of the Barnett Formula - the system that determines how Wales is funded.

Welsh ministers have long called for the Barnett funding formula to be reformed, claiming it disadvantages Wales.

However, it is argued Scotland does well from the formula.

Before he became prime minister, Burnham made the case for change, but on his recent visit to Wales he played down the prospect of reform.

Swinney said: "Financial arrangements across the United Kingdom vary and by constituent part of the United Kingdom. We all have to put forward the issues and the interests and the perspectives in each of our countries."

Ap Iorwerth said: "There are flexibilities that Scotland already have right now as a minimum to be handed to Wales, is something that is important to us."

The dynamics in Wales are different from those in Scotland.

Ap Iorwerth, who was appointed the first non-Labour first minister of Wales after May's Senedd election, had ruled out pushing for a referendum on Welsh independence during his party's first term in government.

His government intends to set up a national commission to "lay the foundations" for future plans for Welsh independence.

In the meantime, Welsh ministers are seeking extra powers to be transferred to Wales, including over policing and youth justice - which Burnham has said he is "open" to the idea of.

Ap Iorwerth said Burnham had "a lot to learn" about "how devolution to a nation is rather different to devolution to a region or a city of England".

"I want to have a positive relationship with him, I believe he wants to have a positive relationship with me," he said.

The UK government said: "The prime minister is committed to delivering change across all four nations of the United Kingdom and believes strongly in the union."

The devolved leaders will meet the prime minister next month.

Labour leader in Wales, Ken Skates, said: "Plaid have given people nothing since the election.

"They clearly want to use power to break up Britain, weaken Wales and spend their time obsessing over more powers for their politicians."

Welsh Conservative Senedd leader Darren Millar said: "Instead of obsessing about independence, the first minister should be focused on dealing with the crisis engulfing the Welsh NHS and the declining standards in Welsh schools."

Dan Thomas, Reform UK's Welsh leader, said: "The first minister can't get a grip of NHS waiting lists or our education system, but apparently has time to tell us what we all know. That he wants the break up the UK."
